questions.prompt: Your regression model has low training error but high validation error. Explain what is happening in bias-variance terms, and name three concrete interventions - including how L1 and L2 regularization differ in their effect on the weights.
questions.modelAnswer: That gap is the signature of high variance: the model has enough capacity to fit noise in the training set, so it generalizes poorly. Interventions: get more training data, reduce effective capacity (simpler model, fewer features, early stopping), or add regularization. L2 adds a squared-weight penalty that shrinks all weights smoothly toward zero but rarely to exactly zero, spreading credit across correlated features; L1 adds an absolute-value penalty whose corner at zero drives many weights exactly to zero, giving sparse models and implicit feature selection. In practice you tune the regularization strength against a validation curve and confirm the train-validation gap closes without training error blowing up, which would signal you have overshot into high bias.
rubric: Correctly identifies the train-validation gap as high variance / overfitting, not bias
States the mechanical difference between L1 (sparsity via corner at zero) and L2 (smooth shrinkage)
Names at least three distinct interventions, not three flavors of one
Mentions validating the fix and the trade-off of overshooting into underfitting
followUps: Why does L1's penalty geometry produce exact zeros while L2's does not?
When would you prefer elastic net over either alone?

questions.prompt: You are building a model on 18 months of customer transaction data. How do you split it for training and evaluation, and what leakage traps do you specifically watch for?
questions.modelAnswer: Split by time, not randomly: train on the earliest window, validate on the next, test on the most recent, because deployment means predicting the future and a random split lets the model peek at it. Watch for group leakage - the same customer appearing in both train and test lets the model memorize identities, so split by customer where the task demands it. Watch for feature-computation leakage: aggregates computed over the full 18 months (lifetime spend, average basket) encode the future into training rows; features must be computed as-of each row's timestamp. Watch for target leakage - fields populated after the outcome, like a chargeback flag when predicting fraud. Finally, fit all preprocessing (scalers, encoders, imputers) on the training window only, and compare distributions across windows so you know how much natural shift the model must survive.
rubric: Chooses a time-based split and justifies it against random splitting
Names at least three distinct leakage classes: group, as-of feature computation, target leakage
States that preprocessing must be fit on the training window only
Connects split design to the deployment assumption of predicting forward in time
followUps: How would you detect leakage you did not anticipate?
When is a random split actually the right choice?

questions.prompt: You are evaluating a fraud model on a dataset with 0.5 percent positives. Why is accuracy misleading here, which metrics do you reach for instead, and how do you choose an operating threshold?
questions.modelAnswer: Predicting 'not fraud' for everything scores 99.5 percent accuracy while catching zero fraud, so accuracy is nearly information-free at this prevalence. Use precision and recall on the positive class, and prefer PR-AUC over ROC-AUC: ROC's false-positive rate has the huge negative class in its denominator, so a model can look excellent on ROC while flooding reviewers with false alarms. The threshold is a business decision, not a modeling one: estimate the cost of a missed fraud versus a false alarm and the capacity of the review team, then, for example, fix a precision floor that keeps the review queue workable and maximize recall subject to it. Calibrate the scores so thresholds are stable and meaningful, and monitor prevalence in production - class balance drifts, and a threshold tuned offline quietly changes its precision-recall trade-off when it does.
rubric: Shows numerically why accuracy degenerates at 0.5 percent prevalence
Justifies PR-AUC over ROC-AUC via the FPR denominator argument, not just by naming it
Ties threshold choice to error costs and review capacity, not a default 0.5
Mentions calibration or prevalence drift as an operational concern
followUps: How does downsampling negatives during training distort calibration, and how do you correct it?

questions.prompt: A teammate benchmarks a model with: X_scaled = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X); scores = cross_val_score(model, X_scaled, y, cv=5). What is wrong, how do you fix it, and which other preprocessing steps carry the same trap - ranked by how badly they bias the score?
questions.modelAnswer: The scaler is fit on all of X before cross-validation, so each validation fold's mean and variance have leaked into the transform applied to its own training folds - the reported score is optimistically biased. The fix is to make preprocessing part of the estimator: pipe = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), model); scores = cross_val_score(pipe, X, y, cv=5), so the scaler is refit inside each fold on that fold's training data only. The same trap applies to any fitted transform: imputation, feature selection, PCA, oversampling like SMOTE, and worst of all target encoding, because it injects label information directly into features - that one can turn a worthless model into an apparently great one. Mean-variance scaling usually biases scores only mildly; label-derived transforms are the ones that fabricate performance. The general rule: anything with a fit method belongs inside the CV loop, and a Pipeline is the mechanism that enforces it.
rubric: Pinpoints that fold statistics leak through the pre-fit scaler and the direction of the bias
Gives the concrete Pipeline fix, not just 'be careful'
Ranks target/label-derived transforms as the severe case versus mild scaling leakage
States the general rule: every fitted transform goes inside the CV loop
followUps: How does nested cross-validation extend this rule to hyperparameter search?

questions.prompt: You have 200k rows and 300 mixed-type features for tabular churn prediction. Compare random forests against gradient boosting for this problem, then lay out your end-to-end modeling approach.
questions.modelAnswer: On tabular data of this shape, gradient boosting (LightGBM/XGBoost) usually wins: it fits trees sequentially on residuals, capturing interactions with high accuracy, while a random forest averages independently grown trees - more robust to hyperparameters and noise, trivially parallel, and a strong baseline, but typically a few points behind a tuned booster. Boosting's costs are sensitivity to noisy labels and leakage, and more tuning surface. My approach: start with logistic regression for a calibrated, interpretable baseline and sanity-check that boosted trees actually beat it; validate with a time-based split since churn is temporal. Then LightGBM with native categorical handling (or target encoding fit strictly inside CV), early stopping on the validation window, and a small search over num_leaves, learning rate, and min_child_samples. Finish with calibration if scores feed decisions, SHAP for stakeholder-facing explanations, and a leakage audit of the top features - in churn, a feature that is too good is usually a symptom of the label leaking in.
rubric: Explains the mechanism difference - sequential residual fitting versus independent averaging - not just tool names
States boosting's trade-offs: noise/leakage sensitivity and tuning surface
Includes a simple calibrated baseline and a temporal validation scheme
Audits suspiciously strong features for leakage before shipping
followUps: When would a linear model beat trees on tabular data?
How do monotonic constraints help with stakeholder trust?

questions.prompt: Your classifier's probabilities are used to decide which customers get a costly retention offer. What does it mean for the model to be calibrated, how do you measure it, and how do you fix miscalibration?
questions.modelAnswer: Calibrated means the probabilities are honest frequencies: among customers scored 0.7, about 70 percent actually churn. That matters here because the offer decision is an expected-value computation - miscalibrated scores systematically mis-spend the budget even if ranking (AUC) is perfect. Measure it with a reliability diagram, expected calibration error, and Brier score on a held-out set. Boosted trees and modern neural nets are often overconfident out of the box, and any class rebalancing during training (up/down-sampling, class weights) distorts calibration further and needs a prior correction. Fix by fitting a post-hoc mapping on held-out data: Platt scaling or temperature scaling for smooth monotone adjustment, isotonic regression when you have enough data for a nonparametric fit. Recheck calibration after deployment - it drifts with the population even when AUC holds steady.
rubric: Defines calibration as predicted probability matching empirical frequency
Explains why the downstream cost decision makes calibration matter beyond AUC
Names measurement tools (reliability diagram, ECE or Brier) and a post-hoc fix fit on held-out data
Flags rebalanced training or drift as calibration hazards to monitor
followUps: Why does isotonic regression overfit on small calibration sets?

questions.prompt: Three epochs into training, your deep network's loss becomes NaN. Walk me through your debugging order and the reasoning behind it.
questions.modelAnswer: First check the data at and just before the failing step: scan the batch for NaN/Inf inputs or targets - data bugs are the most common cause and the cheapest to rule out; reproduce deterministically by seeding and replaying that step. Second, the learning rate: too-high LR is the top training-side cause, so drop it an order of magnitude or add warmup and see whether the divergence moves or disappears. Third, instrument gradient norms per step - a spike before the NaN means exploding gradients, addressed with clipping and a saner init. Fourth, audit numerically unstable ops: log(0) or division by zero in a custom loss, softmax on large logits without a logsumexp formulation, missing epsilons in normalization layers. Fifth, mixed precision: fp16 overflows without proper loss scaling, and switching to bf16 or full fp32 for a run is a fast differential diagnosis. The meta-principle is to bisect - reproduce at the smallest scale that still fails, change one variable at a time, and let logged norms tell you where the explosion starts rather than guessing.
rubric: Checks data for NaN/Inf before touching the model, with a deterministic replay of the failing step
Orders hypotheses by likelihood and cost: data, then LR, then gradients, then numerics, then precision
Names concrete instrumentation: per-step gradient norms, loss scaling checks
Describes bisection - smallest failing reproduction, one variable at a time
followUps: How does bf16 differ from fp16 in overflow behavior, and why does that matter here?
What would make you suspect a single corrupted batch, and how do you find it?

questions.prompt: Offline AUC is 0.91 but deployed precision collapsed within a week. Walk through your debugging order.
questions.modelAnswer: First, training/serving skew: for a sample of recently scored entities, recompute the features offline and diff them against what the service actually saw - a pipeline silently defaulting a feature to null or computing it on a different window is the classic cause of exactly this signature. Second, separate the hypotheses: data drift (input distributions moved), concept drift (the label relationship changed), or a plain pipeline bug, by slicing recent scored traffic against the training distribution and checking the score distribution for sudden shape changes. Third, audit the offline evaluation for leakage - a 0.91 AUC that never survives contact with production frequently means a feature was leaking the label, and the leak simply does not exist at serving time. While diagnosing, put a guardrail in place: roll back to the last-good model and keep a scored holdout so you can compare models on live traffic. Then make the failure impossible to miss next time: feature-distribution alerts, prediction-score distribution monitoring, and delayed-label precision tracking.
rubric: Checks training/serving feature skew first
Distinguishes data drift vs concept drift vs pipeline bug
Proposes a leakage audit of the offline eval
Defines rollback/holdout guardrail
Names monitoring signals to add
followUps: What single dashboard would have caught this in day one rather than week one?

questions.prompt: Design serving for a churn model consumed by a nightly campaign system and an in-app real-time surface. Cover batch versus online scoring, feature freshness, and how you roll out a new model version.
questions.modelAnswer: Split by consumer. The campaign system gets nightly batch scoring: score the full population into a warehouse table - cheap, simple, easy to backfill, and latency-irrelevant. The in-app surface gets an online endpoint, and the key risk there is training/serving skew, so serve features from a feature store whose offline and online paths share one definition; precompute heavy aggregates and keep request-time computation minimal. Rollout: register the model in a versioned registry, shadow-score live traffic to compare distributions against the incumbent, then canary a small percentage with business-metric guardrails and one-click rollback; batch and online must promote from the same registry entry so consumers never disagree about which model is live. Monitor per-path: endpoint latency and error rate, score-distribution divergence between batch and online for the same customers (a direct skew detector), and feature freshness lag. Cost-wise, batch covers the bulk of the need cheaply - keep the online path small and boring.
rubric: Serves each consumer with the appropriate mode instead of one path for both
Addresses training/serving skew with a shared offline/online feature definition
Rollout includes shadow, canary with guardrail metrics, and rollback from a versioned registry
Monitors batch-online score divergence and feature freshness, not just uptime
Notes the cost asymmetry: batch is cheap, online capacity is the expensive part
followUps: Where does a streaming feature pipeline enter this design, and what does it cost you?

questions.prompt: A drift monitor pages you: PSI breached on three key features, and downstream conversion is dipping. Walk me through your first 30 minutes.
questions.modelAnswer: Minute zero: verify the alert is real before acting on it - most 'drift' pages are upstream data incidents, so check pipeline health, join rates, schema changes, and whether a vendor or logging deploy landed; three features breaching together strongly suggests a shared upstream cause rather than the world changing. Next, quantify blast radius: is the score distribution shifted, which segments drive the conversion dip, and does the dip line up in time with the feature shift. If model output is genuinely degraded, mitigate before root-causing: roll back to the previous model if it predates the shift, or fall back to a rules baseline for the affected segment - drift alone is not a reason to retrain blindly, and retraining on corrupted features would bake the incident into the model. Then root-cause: upstream bug versus product change versus real behavior shift, each with a different owner and fix. Close out by logging a timeline, deciding the retrain trigger once trustworthy labels arrive, and tuning the alert so the next page carries the upstream-health context you just had to gather by hand.
rubric: Verifies data-pipeline health before treating the alert as real drift
Reasons that correlated multi-feature breaks imply a shared upstream cause
Mitigates first - rollback or rules fallback - before root-causing or retraining
Explicitly rejects retraining on corrupted features
Ends with alert tuning and a labeled-data retrain trigger
followUps: How do you set PSI thresholds so this alert stays high-precision?

questions.prompt: In one pass: what does a single self-attention head compute, and why did attention displace recurrence for long sequences?
questions.modelAnswer: A head projects each token into query, key, and value vectors, computes attention weights as softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d_k)), and outputs a weighted sum of value vectors - each token gathers a learned, content-based summary of every other position, and multiple heads let different relations be attended in parallel. Attention displaced recurrence for two linked reasons. Computationally, an RNN needs O(n) sequential steps, so training cannot parallelize across the sequence; attention processes all positions at once, which is what made large-scale pretraining economical. For learning, an RNN's gradient between distant tokens must survive n multiplicative steps - the vanishing-gradient path - while attention gives a direct one-hop connection between any two tokens. The price is O(n^2) compute and memory in sequence length, which is why the efficiency work (FlashAttention, sparse and sliding-window variants) exists.
rubric: States the QKV computation including the softmax over scaled dot products
Gives both displacement reasons: parallel training and direct gradient paths
Names the O(n^2) cost as the trade-off attention accepts
Keeps the explanation crisp enough for a two-minute answer
followUps: What does multi-head buy over one big head at equal parameter count?

questions.prompt: Design the retrieval side of a RAG assistant over 50,000 internal PDFs: chunking, embedding and retrieval strategy, and how you will know it actually works.
questions.modelAnswer: Parse with layout awareness - headings, tables, and section boundaries - because garbage extraction caps everything downstream. Chunk to roughly 200-500 tokens along semantic boundaries with modest overlap, and prepend document title and section path to each chunk so embeddings carry context the raw text lacks. Retrieve hybrid: dense embeddings for paraphrase matching plus BM25 for exact terms and identifiers, fused with reciprocal-rank fusion, then a cross-encoder reranks the top ~50 down to the handful that enter the prompt; metadata filters (team, doc type, date) cut the search space and enforce scoping. Evaluate the stages separately: a golden set of question-to-source-passage pairs measures retrieval recall@k independent of generation, then answer faithfulness gets checked against the retrieved context with an LLM judge plus spot-checked human labels. The central trade-off is chunk size - small chunks retrieve precisely but fragment context - which overlap and parent-document expansion mitigate. Per-stage metrics are what make failures debuggable: when quality drops you can say whether retrieval or generation broke.
rubric: Chunking is semantic with context prepended, and the size trade-off is articulated
Retrieval is hybrid dense+lexical with reranking, with a reason for each stage
Evaluation separates retrieval recall from answer faithfulness with a golden set
Mentions metadata filtering or scoping as both a relevance and access lever
followUps: When does fine-tuning the embedding model beat better chunking?
How do tables and figures change your parsing strategy?

questions.prompt: When do you build an agent with tool use versus a single structured LLM call - and what makes agent loops fail in production?
questions.modelAnswer: Use a single structured call when the task is a one-shot mapping with a known output schema - classify, extract, rewrite: it is cheaper, lower-variance, and trivially testable. Reach for an agent only when the task genuinely needs environment feedback: look something up, act on the result, recover from errors, repeat - the loop must earn its cost. Production failure modes are predictable: errors compound across steps, so a 95-percent-reliable step decays fast over many steps; loops fail to terminate, so you cap iterations and spend; tools get misused when their specs are ambiguous, so you write tight JSON schemas and prefer a few well-described tools over many overlapping ones. Side-effecting tools need guardrails - confirmation gates, sandboxing, or dry-run modes - because a wrong retrieval wastes tokens but a wrong write is an incident. And you trace every step with full inputs and outputs, since an untraced agent is undebuggable by construction.
rubric: Gives a crisp decision rule: environment feedback justifies the loop, otherwise single call
Names compounding error and non-termination with concrete mitigations (caps, budgets)
Treats side-effecting tools as a distinct safety class with gates or sandboxing
Insists on per-step tracing as the observability baseline
followUps: How would you measure whether the agent beats a two-call pipeline on your task?

questions.prompt: Sketch the offline eval harness for an LLM feature that drafts support replies: the dataset, the scoring loop, and specifically how you make an LLM judge trustworthy.
questions.modelAnswer: Curate 200-500 real anonymized tickets with reference answers and a written grading rubric, stratified across intents and difficulty, held fixed as a versioned eval set. The harness loop: for each case, generate with pinned model, prompt version, and parameters; score with deterministic checks first - required facts present, format valid, refusals happening exactly where policy demands - because those are free and unambiguous; then an LLM judge scores rubric dimensions like correctness and tone. Judge trustworthiness is earned, not assumed: use a judge model independent of the generator, anchor it to the rubric rather than raw preference, and when comparing two systems swap answer order across paired calls because position bias is real and large. Validate the judge itself by measuring agreement against a human-labeled subset - Cohen's kappa, not just percent agreement - and re-baseline whenever the judge model or rubric changes. Wire the harness into CI so every prompt or model change reports per-slice deltas against the incumbent, and block regressions above a threshold. The pinned versions matter: an eval you cannot reproduce is an anecdote.
rubric: Dataset is real, stratified, versioned, and paired with an explicit rubric
Deterministic checks run before judge scoring, with refusal correctness included
Judge de-biasing is concrete: independent judge, order swapping, rubric anchoring
Judge is validated against human labels with an agreement statistic
Harness runs in CI with per-slice regression gates
followUps: What breaks when you reuse the eval set for prompt tuning week after week?

questions.prompt: Product wants the model to follow a house style and answer questions about your domain. Prompting, RAG, or fine-tuning - how do you decide?
questions.modelAnswer: Order the options by cost and reversibility. Prompting first: style, tone, format, and few-shot patterns usually land with a good system prompt, and iteration is instant. RAG when the model needs knowledge that is private, large, or changing - knowledge that changes does not belong in weights, and retrieval gives you citations and instant updates. Fine-tuning (typically LoRA on an instruct model) earns its place for consistent behavior at scale: reliable format and voice without a huge prompt, lower latency from shorter prompts, or capability the base model genuinely lacks; it is the wrong tool for injecting fresh facts, where it mostly teaches confident hallucination. The decision procedure is empirical: build a small eval set for the actual task, and stop at the cheapest tier that hits the quality bar. Also weigh the ops tail of fine-tuning - training cadence, regression evals, and serving custom weights - which prompting and RAG avoid entirely.
rubric: Presents a cost/reversibility ordering rather than a tool preference
Correctly assigns changing knowledge to RAG and behavior/style to fine-tuning
Rejects fine-tuning as a fact-injection mechanism with the hallucination rationale
Decision is driven by an eval set, and the ops cost of fine-tuning is priced in
followUps: When do prompting and fine-tuning combine rather than compete?

questions.prompt: What layers of guardrails would you put around an LLM feature that can see customer PII, and where does each one run?
questions.modelAnswer: Defense in depth, because no single layer holds. Input layer, before the model call: prompt-injection screening on anything user-supplied or retrieved, and PII minimization - redact or tokenize fields the feature does not strictly need, so the model never holds what it should not leak. Model layer: a hardened system prompt plus least-privilege tool scopes - the model cannot be talked into an action it has no capability for, which is the only injection defense that is structural rather than probabilistic. Output layer: schema validation, PII and policy classifiers on responses, and grounding checks against sources for factual claims. Application layer, outside the model entirely: authorization enforced in code so the model's output cannot widen access, rate limits, and human-in-the-loop for high-stakes actions. Around all of it: full audit logging of inputs, outputs, and tool calls, and recurring red-teaming with injection suites, since guardrails decay as prompts and models change.
rubric: Covers input, model/tool-scope, output, and application layers distinctly
Identifies least-privilege tool scope as structural, versus probabilistic filters
Keeps authorization outside the model rather than trusting model judgment
Includes audit logging and recurring red-team testing as maintenance, not one-off
followUps: Why is retrieved document content an injection surface, and what do you do about it?

questions.prompt: Design an internal document-QA assistant for 5,000 employees over Confluence and Drive, where documents carry per-user permissions. Walk through the architecture and name the hardest problem.
questions.modelAnswer: Ingestion: connectors do incremental sync on change events, parse and chunk documents, embed into a vector store, and - the critical part - carry each source document's ACL as chunk metadata. Query path: authenticate the user, run hybrid retrieval with a permission filter applied inside the query so only chunks the user can read are even candidates, rerank, then generate with mandatory citations. The hardest problem is permissions, and the design rule is filter-before-retrieve: post-filtering after generation is a data leak, because the model has already read the forbidden context, and ACL sync lag is itself a leak window - revocations must propagate on a tight SLO. Retrieved documents are untrusted input, so injection defenses apply to your own corpus. Evaluation: golden-set retrieval recall, faithfulness checks on answers, and a thumbs-down triage loop feeding a fix queue. Operations: index-freshness SLO, per-query cost budget enforced by context caps and embedding caches, and graceful degradation to citation-only search results when generation fails or confidence is low.
rubric: ACLs travel with chunks and filtering happens at query time, with the leak rationale stated
Treats ACL propagation lag as a security SLO, not an eventual-consistency detail
Treats retrieved corpus content as an injection surface
Has a real eval story: retrieval recall, faithfulness, and a feedback triage loop
Includes cost controls and a degraded search-only fallback
followUps: How does the design change at 500k documents and 50k employees?

questions.prompt: After a provider-side model upgrade, hallucination complaints on your RAG product triple overnight. Walk through your response.
questions.modelAnswer: Mitigate first: if the provider allows version pinning, pin back to the prior model - fastest fix and simultaneously the cleanest causal test; if complaints drop, you have your cause. In parallel, reproduce quantitatively: run the frozen eval suite against both versions and diff faithfulness and grounding scores, because 'complaints tripled' needs a measured counterpart before you tune anything. Typical mechanisms for this signature: the new model weighs instructions in retrieved context differently, formats answers in ways that break your grounding checks or citation parsing, or refuses and hedges differently so users read confident filler as fact. If pinning is unavailable, tighten mitigations you control: stricter grounding instructions, require citations for factual claims and suppress uncited ones, and raise output-validation strictness while accepting the recall cost. The durable fix is procedural: provider model changes go through the eval suite in CI and a canary with a hallucination-rate monitor, and auto-upgrades get disabled - a model version bump is a deploy and deserves deploy discipline.
rubric: Pins/rolls back first and uses the rollback as the causal test
Backs anecdotal complaints with a frozen eval-suite diff across versions
Names plausible mechanisms tied to model-behavior change, not vague 'model got worse'
Ends with the process fix: eval-gated, canaried model upgrades and no auto-upgrade
followUps: What belongs in the postmortem's action items beyond 'add evals'?

questions.prompt: Your LLM feature's monthly token bill doubled and p95 latency rose 40 percent - but traffic is flat. Where do you look?
questions.modelAnswer: Decompose: cost = requests x tokens-per-request x unit price; flat traffic and stable pricing means tokens per request grew, so split input from output tokens in your logs - they have different causes. Input growth suspects: conversation history accumulating without truncation, a RAG change adding chunks or fatter chunks, a system-prompt or few-shot edit in a recent deploy. Output growth suspects: a max_tokens or temperature change, or a model/prompt change making answers rambling - and output tokens are generated serially, so p95 latency rising together with cost points strongly at longer generations. Also check retry storms: timeouts triggering duplicate calls inflate cost and latency while request counts look flat if you count client-side. Diff prompt templates and config by deploy date against the cost inflection. Fixes follow the diagnosis: history truncation or summarization, chunk caps, max_tokens discipline, prompt caching for shared prefixes. Then make it observable: per-feature token dashboards split by input/output, and budget alerts so the next doubling pages you before finance does.
rubric: Decomposes cost arithmetically and isolates tokens-per-request as the moving part
Splits input versus output token growth with distinct suspect lists
Connects output-token growth to serial decode latency to explain the p95 rise
Checks retry amplification, not just prompt size
Closes the loop with token dashboards and budget alerts
followUps: How does prompt caching change the economics of long system prompts?

questions.prompt: A teammate says 'I can't reproduce last month's model.' What should your platform have captured, per training run, to make that sentence impossible?
questions.modelAnswer: Full lineage, captured automatically rather than by discipline: the exact data version (an immutable snapshot or a deterministic query pinned to a data version), the code commit, the resolved config and hyperparameters, the environment as a container image digest plus locked dependency versions, random seeds, and the resulting artifact with its metrics - all linked to one run ID in an experiment tracker and model registry. The sneaky omission is feature definitions: if the feature pipeline changed between then and now, identical training code produces a different model, so feature transformations need versioning too. Artifacts should be content-addressed so 'the model from run X' is unambiguous. One honest caveat: bit-exact reproduction is often impractical because GPU kernels are nondeterministic, so the platform should target statistical reproducibility - same data, code, and config reproducing metrics within a stated tolerance - and say so explicitly.
rubric: Enumerates data version, code, config, environment digest, seeds, and artifact linked to a run ID
Calls out feature-definition versioning as the commonly missed dependency
Distinguishes bit-exact from statistical reproducibility with the GPU nondeterminism caveat
Frames capture as automatic platform behavior, not engineer discipline
followUps: What does content-addressing artifacts buy over naming conventions?

questions.prompt: Design the orchestration for a weekly retraining pipeline - data validation, training, evaluation, deployment - that runs with humans out of the loop unless something is actually wrong.
questions.modelAnswer: Model it as a DAG in an orchestrator (Airflow, Dagster, or Kubeflow), with every step idempotent and retry-safe, and artifacts passed by reference rather than through the scheduler. Gates do the human-replacement work. Gate one, data validation before any GPU is spent: schema, row volume, null rates, and distribution checks against expectations - fail fast here and the pipeline stops cheap. Gate two, evaluation: score the candidate against the current champion on a fixed benchmark set plus a fresh window, and promote only if it clears the champion within guardrail metrics, which is what stops silent quality regressions from shipping on schedule. Gate three, deployment: automatic canary with metric monitors and auto-rollback. The design distinction that keeps pages meaningful: infrastructure failures retry silently, quality-gate failures page a human - inverting that either spams the on-call or ships bad models quietly. Add run lineage for audit, and first-class backfill support, because the first real incident will demand rerunning history with a fixed pipeline.
rubric: Steps are idempotent with artifacts by reference, enabling safe retries and backfills
Data validation gates before training spend - cost-aware ordering
Promotion is champion/challenger with guardrails, not train-then-ship
Separates retryable infra failure from human-paging quality failure
Deployment is canaried with auto-rollback
followUps: How do you test the pipeline itself, as opposed to the models it produces?

questions.prompt: Traffic to a model service spikes 5x in ten minutes; p99 goes from 80ms to 4 seconds and autoscaling is not keeping up. What do you do right now, and how do you prevent the recurrence?
questions.modelAnswer: Right now: protect the core with load shedding - rate-limit or drop low-priority callers, serve a degraded fallback (cached or default scores) where the product tolerates it, and manually raise max replicas while checking what is actually saturated: CPU, GPU, or queue depth, because scaling on the wrong signal is why autoscaling 'is not keeping up.' The usual mechanical culprit is cold start: image pull plus model load takes minutes, so new replicas arrive long after the queue has already ballooned - and a replica that reports ready before weights are loaded makes it worse by absorbing traffic it cannot serve. Prevention: scale on leading signals like queue depth or in-flight concurrency rather than lagging CPU averages, keep a warm pool or overprovisioned headroom sized to your spike profile, shrink images and move model load into the readiness probe so ready means serving, and load-test to find the throughput knee so capacity numbers are measured rather than hoped. Finally, put circuit breakers in upstream clients so the next spike degrades gracefully instead of cascading.
rubric: Immediate actions shed load and add capacity in parallel, identifying the saturated resource

questions.prompt: Your team's training image takes 20 minutes to rebuild after every code change and weighs 8GB. What is likely wrong with the Dockerfile, and how do layering and cache mechanics fix it?
questions.modelAnswer: Docker caches per instruction, and the cache invalidates from the first changed layer downward. The classic mistake is COPY . . before dependency installation: every code edit invalidates the copy layer, so pip install reruns from scratch - that is the 20 minutes. Reorder so the lockfile or requirements file is copied alone, dependencies install as their own cached layer, and application code copies last; code changes then rebuild in seconds. For the 8GB: use a slim or runtime base (a CUDA devel image where runtime suffices is gigabytes of compiler toolchain shipped for nothing), multi-stage builds so build tools never reach the final image, clean package caches in the same RUN instruction that created them - deletion in a later layer hides files but shrinks nothing - and a .dockerignore that keeps datasets, checkpoints, and .git out of the build context. Done right, rebuilds hit cache except the code layer and the image drops to what the runtime actually needs.
rubric: Explains cache invalidation order and the COPY-before-install mistake specifically
Gives the reorder fix: dependencies as a cached layer, code copied last
Names at least two size levers with correct layer mechanics (same-RUN cleanup, multi-stage)
Mentions build-context hygiene via .dockerignore
followUps: What changes when CI builds on ephemeral runners with no local cache?

questions.prompt: Write the essential parts of a Kubernetes Job spec for a single-GPU training run, and explain how resource requests and limits work for GPUs versus CPU and memory.
questions.modelAnswer: Skeleton: apiVersion batch/v1, kind Job; spec.backoffLimit small (2-3) so a deterministic crash does not retry all night; activeDeadlineSeconds to kill hung runs; template with restartPolicy OnFailure; the container with image, command, and resources; plus a nodeSelector or toleration targeting the GPU pool, and volumes for dataset access and checkpoint output. GPUs are requested as resources.limits with nvidia.com/gpu: 1 - extended resources are integer-only and not overcommittable, so requests equal limits and a container either owns the whole device or does not run. CPU and memory differ: requests drive scheduling and limits cap usage, and for training I set memory request equal to limit sized above peak dataloader plus host-memory footprint, because a pod over its memory limit is OOM-killed mid-epoch with no soft-fail. Checkpoints must go to remote storage - pods are ephemeral and a Job retry on a fresh node should resume, not restart. If it must survive preemption, checkpoint-resume logic in the training code matters more than anything in the YAML.
rubric: Spec includes Job-level safety: backoffLimit, activeDeadlineSeconds, restartPolicy
States GPU semantics correctly: integer extended resource in limits, no overcommit

questions.prompt: Your org trains on Slurm and serves on Kubernetes. Why is that split so common - what does each scheduler actually do better?
questions.modelAnswer: They optimize for different contracts. Slurm does gang scheduling natively: a 64-GPU distributed job gets all its allocation atomically or waits - which NCCL-coupled training requires, since a partial allocation deadlocks - plus fair-share accounting across research groups, topology-aware placement, and batch-queue semantics born in HPC. Kubernetes is built around long-running services: rolling deploys, health probes, autoscaling, service discovery, and self-healing, which is exactly the serving problem; but its default scheduler places pods one at a time, so large multi-pod training jobs can partially schedule and starve without add-ons like Volcano or Kueue retrofitting gang semantics. The two worlds are converging - K8s-plus-Kueue training stacks are increasingly credible at moderate scale - but the workload-to-scheduler logic stands: tightly coupled all-or-nothing allocation and queue fairness favor Slurm; elastic, traffic-driven, health-checked services favor Kubernetes. Running both and meeting at the artifact registry is a rational architecture, with the cost of two operational stacks.
rubric: Explains gang scheduling and why partial allocation breaks distributed training
Names fair-share and topology awareness as Slurm strengths beyond gang semantics
Credits K8s with the service lifecycle: probes, rollouts, autoscaling
Acknowledges convergence (Volcano/Kueue) and the two-stack operational cost

questions.prompt: You need to fine-tune a 13B-parameter model on a single node with 8x80GB GPUs. Walk through the memory math and choose a parallelism and optimization strategy.
questions.modelAnswer: Start with the accounting for a full fine-tune with Adam in mixed precision: roughly 16 bytes per parameter - 2 for bf16 weights, 2 for gradients, and 12 for optimizer state (fp32 master weights plus two moments) - so 13B x 16 is about 208GB of state before activations, which no single 80GB GPU holds. Two credible strategies. One: shard with FSDP or ZeRO-3, splitting parameters, gradients, and optimizer state across the 8 GPUs for roughly 26GB of state per GPU, leaving room for activations with activation checkpointing; intra-node NVLink keeps the all-gather overhead tolerable, and no inter-node traffic exists on one node. Two: LoRA - freeze the base weights (13B x 2 bytes = 26GB in bf16, fits per GPU), train low-rank adapters so gradient and optimizer memory collapse to the adapter's few dozen million parameters, and run simple data parallelism; QLoRA quantizes the frozen base to 4-bit if you want more activation headroom. I would default to LoRA unless the task demands deep behavioral change - about an order of magnitude cheaper, easier to serve as swappable adapters, and near-parity quality on most fine-tunes - and reach for FSDP full fine-tuning when eval evidence says adapters are not enough.
rubric: Gets the 16-bytes-per-param accounting right and concludes single-GPU infeasibility

questions.prompt: GPU spend doubled this quarter. As the platform team, what are your biggest levers to cut it without blocking research teams?
questions.modelAnswer: Measure before cutting: per-team, per-job attribution and utilization dashboards, and measure real utilization - SM occupancy and memory bandwidth, not just 'GPU allocated' - because the usual finding is that allocation is high while true utilization sits under 50 percent: grab-and-hold reservations, idle dev boxes overnight, and input-bound jobs starving expensive silicon. Levers in rough order of return: replace static allocation with quota-plus-queue scheduling (Kueue or Slurm) so idle capacity returns to a shared pool; move fault-tolerant training to spot or preemptible instances with mandatory checkpointing, at a large discount; right-size - plenty of jobs on H100s would run fine on cheaper parts; autoscale serving down and consolidate small models onto shared multi-model servers; TTL-reap idle notebooks and stale reservations. The behavioral lever is showback or chargeback - visible cost per team changes habits faster than any scheduler policy. Verify each lever with the same utilization metrics you started from, so savings are demonstrated rather than asserted.
rubric: Starts from attribution and true utilization (SM occupancy), not allocation counts

questions.prompt: A training job on one node runs 3x slower than the identical job did last week. You can SSH in. What do you check, in what order?
questions.modelAnswer: nvidia-smi first, because GPU utilization splits the problem in half: low and choppy utilization means the GPUs are starved and the bottleneck is the input path; high utilization means the compute itself changed. If starved: iostat and iowait for storage trouble - dataset moved to slower storage, cold cache, degraded network filesystem - then CPU saturation in the dataloader (num_workers, preprocessing regressions). If compute-side: nvidia-smi -q for clock throttling, power capping, and thermal state, dmesg for ECC errors and OOM kills, and then the software environment - driver, CUDA, cuDNN, framework versions - since a library upgrade that swaps kernels is a classic silent 3x. Also check for neighbors: on shared nodes, another job contending for the same storage or CPUs produces exactly this signature while your job's code is blameless. To converge fast, run a fixed synthetic-data benchmark that takes storage out of the loop: if synthetic runs at full speed, it is the data path; if not, it is the node or the environment. Diff against last week's run metadata - the answer is usually in what changed, and lineage tells you what did.
rubric: Uses GPU utilization as the first bisection between input-bound and compute-bound

questions.prompt: Table orders(customer_id, order_date, amount). Write SQL returning each customer's two most recent orders, and explain ROW_NUMBER versus RANK versus DENSE_RANK - including the determinism trap.
questions.modelAnswer: SELECT customer_id, order_date, amount FROM (SELECT o.*, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date DESC) AS rn FROM orders o) t WHERE rn <= 2. The subquery (or CTE) is required because window functions are evaluated after WHERE, so you cannot filter on rn in the same query level. The three functions differ only on ties: ROW_NUMBER always emits unique 1..n, arbitrarily breaking ties; RANK gives tied rows the same rank and then skips (1,1,3); DENSE_RANK gives ties the same rank without gaps (1,1,2). The trap: with tied order_dates, ROW_NUMBER's choice of which row is 'second' is nondeterministic and can differ between runs, so a correct query adds a unique tiebreaker to the ordering - ORDER BY order_date DESC, order_id DESC - to make results stable. If the requirement is 'all orders on the two most recent dates,' DENSE_RANK is the right tool instead.
rubric: Query is correct: partition by customer, order descending, filter in an outer level

questions.prompt: Design an A/B test for a checkout-flow change where the team hopes for a 2 percent relative lift in conversion. Cover sizing, randomization, guardrails, and your stopping rule.
questions.modelAnswer: Define the primary metric precisely - conversion per assigned user, intention-to-treat - plus guardrails: revenue per user, latency, and error rate, so a conversion win cannot smuggle in a regression elsewhere. Randomize by user with a stable hash at the assignment point, so a user keeps one experience across sessions. Size it honestly: with a baseline conversion rate, a 2 percent relative MDE, alpha 0.05 and power 0.8, the required sample is large - small relative effects on conversion rates routinely demand hundreds of thousands of users per arm - so compute N up front and report the run length in weeks; run whole weeks to average over weekly cycles. While running: an automated sample-ratio-mismatch check before anyone reads metrics, and no peeking at naive p-values - repeated looks inflate false positives badly, so either fix the horizon or use a sequential method designed for monitoring. Stop at the planned N, analyze ITT, correct for multiple comparisons on secondary metrics and segments, and make the ship decision on effect size with confidence intervals plus guardrail status - not on whether p crossed 0.05 alone.
rubric: Assumptions are explicit: ITT primary metric, stable user-level randomization
Sizing connects MDE, alpha, and power, with an honest run-length implication
Names peeking inflation and offers a legitimate alternative (fixed horizon or sequential)
Includes SRM as an automated validity gate and guardrail metrics in the ship decision
Decision framed on effect size and CIs, not p-value alone
followUps: When would you use CUPED or a variance-reduction technique here?

questions.prompt: Leadership wants 'an engagement metric' for a new feed feature. Walk through your criteria for defining a good one.
questions.modelAnswer: Start from the decision the metric will drive - a metric nobody acts on is decoration. Then define it as a behavior plausibly linked to long-term value, not a vanity count: sessions with a meaningful interaction, say, rather than raw impressions. My criteria: sensitivity, so it moves when the product genuinely changes; robustness to gaming, because Goodhart is real - time-on-feed rewards infinite-scroll traps; attributability to the feature rather than site-wide noise; cheap and timely to compute; and a deliberate denominator - per active user, per session, per exposed user - since most metric disputes are secretly denominator disputes. Validate empirically before adopting: does the candidate correlate with retention in historical data, and does it move sensibly in past experiments you already trust? Pair the north star with guardrails - report rate, unsubscribes, content diversity - and pre-register the definition so it cannot be quietly redefined after results arrive.
rubric: Anchors the metric to a decision and to long-term value, rejecting vanity counts

Validates the candidate against historical retention and trusted past experiments

questions.prompt: A key feature is missing in 30 percent of rows. How does the missingness mechanism change what you do about it?
questions.modelAnswer: Diagnose the mechanism first, because it determines what is statistically defensible. MCAR - missingness unrelated to anything - makes deletion unbiased but wasteful at 30 percent. MAR - missingness explained by other observed variables - justifies model-based or conditional imputation. MNAR - missingness depending on the unobserved value itself, like high earners declining to report income - means any imputation from observed data is biased, and you need domain handling or explicit sensitivity analysis. Practically: test whether missingness correlates with other features or the target; if it does, the missingness is itself signal, so add an indicator flag - and tree models can split on missingness natively. For predictive work, impute inside CV folds only (an imputer fit on all data leaks), never impute the target, and report a sensitivity check showing whether conclusions survive different treatments. At 30 percent, the honest answer often includes fixing collection upstream rather than modeling around it.
rubric: Defines MCAR/MAR/MNAR with the consequence each has for handling
Treats missingness as potential signal with indicator flags
Keeps imputation inside CV folds and off the target
Includes sensitivity analysis or upstream fix as the mature options
followUps: How would you empirically argue a feature is MNAR when the missing values are unobservable?

questions.prompt: You regress sales on ad spend and get a coefficient of 3.2; adding seasonality controls drops it to 0.9. Interpret both numbers, and explain what still stops you from calling 0.9 causal.
questions.modelAnswer: The 3.2 was confounded: ad budgets rise in high seasons and sales rise in high seasons anyway, so the raw coefficient absorbed the seasonal effect and attributed it to advertising. The 0.9 is the association between spend and sales net of the seasonal controls - a better estimate, and the drop itself is informative about how much confounding the controls removed. But 0.9 is still not causal: unobserved confounders remain (competitor actions, pricing, other campaigns), reverse causality is live if budgets are set from sales forecasts, and controlling can itself mislead if a control is a mediator or collider on the causal path. Mechanically, correlated controls also inflate coefficient variance - check VIFs and report confidence intervals rather than the point estimate alone. A causal claim needs identification: a geo-holdout experiment is the gold standard for ad effectiveness, or quasi-experimental designs - instrumental variables, difference-in-differences around exogenous budget changes - when experiments are off the table.
rubric: Explains the coefficient drop as removed confounding, interpreting both numbers
Names at least two remaining threats: unobserved confounding, reverse causality, bad controls
Mentions multicollinearity/VIF and reporting CIs over point estimates
Offers a real identification path: experiment or quasi-experimental design
followUps: What makes a variable a bad control, and how would you spot one here?

questions.prompt: Your test returns p = 0.03. What does that number actually mean - and give two common misreadings you would correct in a stakeholder meeting.
questions.modelAnswer: p = 0.03 means: if the null hypothesis were true, data at least this extreme would occur about 3 percent of the time - it is a statement about the data under an assumed null, not about the hypothesis. Misreading one: 'there is a 3 percent chance the null is true.' Inverting the conditional requires a prior; that is a Bayesian posterior, and a p-value is not one. Misreading two: 'there is a 97 percent chance this replicates' or 'the effect is real' - p-values say nothing direct about replication probability or truth. A third correction worth making: significance is not size - with large samples, trivially small effects produce tiny p-values, so the business question is the effect size with its confidence interval, which shows the range of effects consistent with the data. And the CI has its own subtlety: 95 percent refers to the long-run coverage of the procedure, not a 95 percent probability that this particular interval contains the truth. Decisions should weigh effect size against costs; p alone is not a decision rule.
rubric: Defines the p-value as tail probability of the data under the null
Corrects both inversions: probability null is true, probability of replication
Separates significance from effect size, pushing toward CIs
States CI coverage correctly as a property of the procedure
followUps: When is a Bayesian statement of the form stakeholders actually want available?

questions.prompt: Your A/B dashboard shows treatment winning by 4 percent - but the split is 52/48 instead of the designed 50/50. What do you do?
questions.modelAnswer: Stop the readout: that is a sample-ratio mismatch, and at experiment scale a 52/48 split under a fair 50/50 design is astronomically unlikely - a chi-square test against the designed ratio confirms in one line. SRM means the assignment or logging mechanism is broken, and the breakage is almost never random with respect to outcome, so the +4 percent is untrustworthy in either direction - do not ship on it, and do not 'adjust' for it statistically. Root-cause the mechanism: assignment bugs and hash edge cases, redirects or timeouts that drop treatment users before logging (users who crash out of a slow treatment vanish from the denominator, flattering the survivors), bot filtering hitting arms asymmetrically, or mid-flight configuration changes. Segment the imbalance - by platform, browser, entry point, and date - because where the deficit concentrates usually names the culprit. Then fix and rerun the experiment. The durable lesson: SRM should be an automated gate that blocks the dashboard, not a thing an analyst notices in week two.
rubric: Recognizes SRM and can verify it with a chi-square against the designed ratio
Refuses to interpret the lift, with the selection-bias reasoning stated
Lists plausible mechanisms including differential logging loss
Segments the imbalance to localize the cause, and gates future readouts automatically
followUps: Why does conditioning the analysis on logged-in users not rescue the experiment?

questions.prompt: Monday 9am: the executive dashboard shows DAU down 30 percent overnight. Walk through your first hour.
questions.modelAnswer: Data before drama: a 30 percent overnight cliff is far more often a data incident than a user exodus. First 15 minutes: check pipeline health - ETL job status, late-arriving partitions, upstream schema changes - and the tracking side: did an app release or SDK/tag change ship that could drop event logging? Cross-check against an independent source such as server-side request logs versus client analytics; real drops appear in both, instrumentation breaks disagree. Next: slice by platform, app version, country, and acquisition source - a uniform drop across all slices smells like measurement, a drop concentrated in one Android version smells like a broken release. Check the deploy and release calendar for anything landing at the inflection time. Then communicate: if it is instrumentation, annotate the dashboard immediately - the real damage is executives making decisions on bad numbers - with a correction and backfill plan; if it looks real, escalate with the slices attached so the owning team starts in the right place. Postmortem regardless: freshness and volume monitors on the events feeding this dashboard, paging the data team before the executives see it.
rubric: Leads with the base rate: overnight cliffs are usually pipeline or tracking breaks
Cross-validates against an independent data source
Slices to distinguish uniform (measurement) from concentrated (real) drops

questions.prompt: Design the pipeline that turns raw product events into the company's trusted metrics. What separates a trustworthy pipeline from one that merely functions?
questions.modelAnswer: Structure it in layers: immutable raw event log, staged and cleaned tables, then a dimensional and metric layer - with every transformation versioned in code, dbt-style, rather than living in dashboard SQL where it forks silently. Trust is a set of specific mechanisms. Contracts on event schemas, so producers cannot rename a field and quietly zero a metric downstream. Data tests at each layer boundary - volume, null rates, distributions, referential integrity - that block promotion on failure rather than emailing a warning nobody reads. A semantic layer with certified metric definitions, one owner per metric, so 'revenue' has exactly one meaning; competing definitions are how organizations argue about arithmetic. Lineage and freshness SLAs visible to consumers, so every dashboard says what it depends on and how stale it is. Idempotent, partitioned processing so backfills are routine rather than heroic. Governance: PII isolated with access controls and retention policies. And observability on the metrics themselves - anomaly detection paging the owning team - because the trust-killer is consumers discovering breakage in a Monday meeting before the data team knows.
rubric: Layered architecture with transformations versioned in code, not dashboards
Schema contracts plus promotion-blocking data tests at layer boundaries

Anomaly detection pages the owner before consumers notice
followUps: How do you migrate an org off five conflicting revenue definitions without a war?

questions.prompt: Why does attention divide QK^T by sqrt(d_k) before the softmax - and what actually goes wrong if you leave it out?
questions.modelAnswer: The dot product of two d_k-dimensional vectors with roughly unit-variance components has variance that grows linearly with d_k, so raw attention logits get larger as head dimension grows. Large logits push the softmax into saturation: the distribution collapses toward one-hot, and because softmax gradients scale with p(1-p), gradients through near-saturated attention nearly vanish - early training stalls or destabilizes, and the effect worsens with bigger d_k. Dividing by sqrt(d_k) normalizes the logit variance to be roughly 1 at initialization, keeping the softmax in its responsive regime where attention patterns can actually be learned. Leaving it out is survivable at tiny head dimensions and increasingly damaging at realistic ones. The same logits-scale reasoning shows up across the stack - temperature scaling, logit soft-capping, and initialization schemes are all managing the same softmax-saturation failure mode.
rubric: States the variance-grows-with-d_k argument for dot-product logits

followUps: Why does the problem bite at initialization specifically?

questions.prompt: How does BPE tokenization work, and give three concrete ways tokenizer choice shows up in production LLM cost or quality.
questions.modelAnswer: Byte-pair encoding starts from a base alphabet of bytes or characters and repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pair in the training corpus into a new vocabulary token; encoding applies those learned merges, so common words become single tokens while rare strings fragment into many. Production consequences: first, cost and latency are denominated in tokens, and fertility - tokens per word - varies sharply by language, so non-English text often costs two to four times more per character and burns context faster, a direct pricing and UX issue for multilingual products. Second, domain mismatch: jargon, code identifiers, or medical terms absent from tokenizer training fragment badly, degrading both quality and effective context length; whitespace and number handling similarly shape code and arithmetic performance, since a model that sees digits chunked inconsistently struggles with digit-level manipulation. Third, operational sharp edges: budgets and truncation must be computed in tokens not characters, and string-level filters can miss content that crosses token boundaries. That is why tokenizer choice is a day-one architectural decision - it is effectively frozen into the model.
rubric: Describes the merge-based BPE algorithm correctly in brief

questions.prompt: A 7B decoder serves 32 concurrent requests at 4k context, fp16 KV cache, 32 layers, 32 heads, head_dim 128. Walk through the KV-cache memory estimate and name two levers to cut it.
questions.modelAnswer: Per token, each layer stores both K and V: 2 x 32 layers x 32 heads x 128 head_dim x 2 bytes (fp16) = 524,288 bytes, about 0.5 MB per token. At 4k context that is roughly 2 GB per request, and at 32 concurrent requests roughly 64 GB - the KV cache, not the 14 GB of fp16 weights, is what dominates memory at high concurrency. Levers: GQA/MQA shares K/V heads across query heads, cutting the head count in the formula - 8 KV heads instead of 32 is a 4x reduction with minimal quality loss; KV-cache quantization to fp8 or int8 halves it again; paged attention eliminates fragmentation and over-allocation from reserving max-length buffers; and context policies - sliding windows, eviction, prefix/prompt caching - cut the cached tokens themselves. Each lever trades a little quality or engineering complexity for large capacity gains, and they compose.
rubric: States the per-token KV formula counting both K and V
Reaches ~64 GB order of magnitude with unit tracking
Names at least 2 reduction levers
Notes each lever's quality/throughput trade-off

questions.prompt: What do MQA and GQA change relative to standard multi-head attention, and why did GQA become the default in serving-oriented models?
questions.modelAnswer: In standard MHA, each of the H query heads has its own K and V heads, so the KV cache scales with H. MQA keeps H query heads but shares a single K/V head across all of them - an H-fold KV-cache reduction; GQA interpolates, grouping query heads to share a smaller set of KV heads, for example 32 query heads over 8 KV heads for a 4x reduction. This matters doubly at serving time: the KV cache is the concurrency bottleneck, and decode is memory-bandwidth-bound, so reading a smaller cache each step speeds token generation as well as fitting more requests. MQA's aggressive sharing costs measurable quality on some tasks; GQA recovers nearly all of it while keeping most of the memory and bandwidth win, which is why Llama-class serving-oriented models standardized on it. A practical bonus: an existing MHA checkpoint can be uptrained to GQA by mean-pooling KV heads with a comparatively small amount of continued training, far cheaper than pretraining with the choice baked in.
rubric: Correctly locates the change in KV heads shared across query heads
Quantifies the cache reduction (H-fold for MQA, H/groups for GQA)

questions.prompt: Estimate the parameter count: decoder-only transformer, d_model 4096, 32 layers, vocab 50k, FFN expansion 4x, tied embeddings; ignore biases and LayerNorm. Show the arithmetic - then, roughly what training-token budget would Chinchilla-style scaling suggest?
questions.modelAnswer: Per layer, attention has four d x d projections (Q, K, V, output): 4 x 4096^2 = 67,108,864. The FFN at 4x expansion has two matrices, d x 4d up and 4d x d down: 8 x 4096^2 = 134,217,728. So 12 x d^2 = 201,326,592 per layer, and 32 layers gives about 6.44B. The tied embedding adds 50,000 x 4096 = 204,800,000, about 0.2B, counted once because input and output embeddings share weights. Total roughly 6.6B - a 7B-class model, and the useful heuristic to carry: non-embedding parameters are about 12 x layers x d_model^2 for a 4x-FFN architecture. Chinchilla-style compute-optimal scaling suggests around 20 tokens per parameter, so on the order of 130B training tokens for this model. Modern practice deliberately overtrains far past that - Llama-class models see trillions of tokens - because training compute is paid once while inference cost scales with model size forever, so a smaller model trained longer wins on lifetime economics.

questions.prompt: Compare PPO-based RLHF with DPO for aligning a chat model: what does each optimize, and when would you pick one over the other?
questions.modelAnswer: RLHF is a two-stage pipeline: fit a reward model on human preference pairs, then run PPO to maximize that reward with a KL penalty keeping the policy near the reference model. It is flexible and online - the policy samples fresh outputs and can be pushed beyond the preference data's support - but operationally heavy: policy, reference, reward model, and value function in memory, PPO's hyperparameter fragility, and reward hacking as a standing threat. DPO collapses the pipeline: for the same KL-regularized objective there is a closed-form relationship between the optimal policy and the reward, so you can optimize the policy directly on preference pairs with a simple classification-style loss - no reward model, no sampling loop, dramatically simpler and more stable. Its limits are the mirror image: it is offline, bound to the support and quality of the preference dataset, and can drift if the data is far off-policy. Practical rule: DPO and its variants for most teams and most fine-tunes; online RL when you have the infrastructure and need to optimize against a reward signal beyond static pairs. In both cases the binding constraint is preference-data quality and evaluation coverage, not the algorithm.
rubric: Describes both objectives correctly, including the KL anchor to the reference model
