questions.prompt: You serve a 70B model and want to cut serving cost with quantization. Design the approach: what do you quantize, with which class of method, and how do you validate it?
questions.modelAnswer: First separate the two regimes. Weight-only quantization (int4 GPTQ/AWQ-class) shrinks memory about 4x versus fp16 and speeds up decode, which is memory-bandwidth-bound - ideal when you are capacity- or VRAM-constrained. Weight-and-activation quantization (fp8 on Hopper-class hardware, or SmoothQuant-style int8) engages faster tensor-core math, accelerating compute-bound prefill too - the better default when you control modern hardware. My plan: fp8 W8A8 as the baseline on H100s, int4 weight-only where memory is the binding constraint; keep the sensitive pieces - embeddings, lm_head, and often the first and last blocks - at higher precision, and quantize the KV cache to fp8 as a separate, composable lever. Validation is where quantization efforts fail: perplexity deltas are necessary but not sufficient, so run the full task-eval suite plus format and safety regressions against the fp16 baseline and inspect per-task deltas, because long-tail degradation - non-English, math, strict-format outputs - hides inside healthy aggregates. Then benchmark end-to-end throughput and latency to confirm the win is real on your serving stack, and roll out behind a flag with quality monitors and an A/B, keeping instant rollback to the fp16 path.
rubric: Distinguishes weight-only vs weight+activation and maps each to decode vs prefill economics
Keeps sensitive components at higher precision and treats KV quantization as separate
Validation goes beyond perplexity to per-task, format, and safety regressions
Confirms the cost win with end-to-end benchmarks and ships behind a flag with rollback
followUps: Why do outlier activation channels make int8 activation quantization hard?

questions.prompt: Design an LLM inference service to hold TTFT p95 under 500ms and inter-token p95 under 50ms at 100 requests per second. Cover batching, scheduling, and capacity planning.
questions.modelAnswer: Anchor on the two-phase reality: prefill is compute-bound and produces TTFT; decode is memory-bandwidth-bound and produces inter-token latency - one SLO per phase, so measure and protect them separately. The core throughput mechanism is continuous batching: the scheduler admits and retires requests at token-step granularity, so new arrivals join between decode iterations instead of waiting for a static batch to drain. The tension is that a long prefill inserted into the decode loop stalls every in-flight request's next token, so chunk prefills into slices interleaved with decode steps, and at scale disaggregate - separate prefill and decode pools with KV handoff - to isolate the SLOs completely. Memory: paged KV cache to prevent fragmentation, and admission control against a KV budget so overload queues at the door rather than OOMing mid-stream. Capacity: benchmark one replica for tokens/sec and max concurrent sequences at the target latency point - not at max throughput, which sits past the latency knee - then provision for peak with headroom and autoscale on queue depth and KV utilization, draining connections on scale-down. Add prompt caching for shared prefixes, priority classes with a dedicated long-context pool so heavy requests cannot blow the p95, and load-shedding that rejects early with a clear signal. Observability: per-phase histograms of TTFT and TPOT, KV occupancy, preemption counts, and queue depth - these are the dials the on-call actually turns.
rubric: Separates prefill/TTFT from decode/TPOT and treats them as distinct SLOs
Explains continuous batching and the prefill-stalls-decode tension with a mitigation
Uses paged KV plus KV-budget admission control to fail at the door, not mid-stream
Capacity is benchmarked at the latency point with autoscaling on leading signals
Includes priority isolation for long-context and per-phase observability
followUps: Where does speculative decoding fit, and what does it do to your capacity math?

questions.prompt: Your benchmark shows TTFT holding steady but inter-token latency degrading 3x once concurrency passes 16. What is happening, and how do you confirm it?
questions.modelAnswer: The signature points at the decode path: every decode step processes the whole batch, and each step must read every sequence's KV cache, so total KV bytes read per token-step grows with concurrency - past a knee you saturate memory bandwidth and per-token time climbs while prefill (compute-bound, unchanged) keeps TTFT flat. Three specific suspects: pure bandwidth saturation from aggregate KV size; KV-cache pressure triggering preemptions or swapping, which shows up as latency spikes rather than smooth degradation - check the engine's preemption and eviction counters; and prefill interleaving stalling decode if chunked prefill is off, though that usually moves TTFT too. Confirm by measurement: sweep concurrency and plot per-token latency against total batched tokens - a bandwidth story bends at a predictable knee; profile with DCGM or Nsight expecting high memory-bandwidth utilization with comparatively low SM occupancy during decode; and correlate the latency curve with KV occupancy and preemption metrics. Fixes follow the diagnosis: cap max batched tokens per step to bound worst-case step time, enable chunked prefill, shrink KV traffic with GQA or fp8 KV quantization, or accept the knee as your per-replica capacity and scale out - often the honest answer is that 16 concurrent sequences is simply this hardware's operating point.
rubric: Explains why decode degrades with batch KV growth while TTFT stays flat
Separates smooth bandwidth saturation from spiky preemption/eviction behavior
Confirms with profiler evidence: bandwidth-bound decode, preemption counters, latency-vs-tokens curve
Fixes match the mechanism, including accepting the knee as capacity
followUps: How would you design the benchmark to find this knee before production did?

questions.prompt: An hour after a routine deploy, your self-hosted LLM API starts throwing intermittent CUDA OOMs and occasionally garbled outputs. Walk through your incident response.
questions.modelAnswer: Mitigate first: roll back the deploy - a failure starting an hour after a change is presumed caused by it until proven otherwise - and recycle the affected replicas rather than trusting them, because a process that has hit CUDA OOM can be left with a corrupted allocator or fragmented memory, and garbled output from a wounded process does not heal on its own. If rollback is blocked, reduce pressure: cut max concurrency and max context so requests stop landing past the memory budget. Then diagnose from the diff and the telemetry: what changed - engine version, weights, or config - with special suspicion of lost admission-control settings (max batched tokens, KV budget), since 'intermittent OOM correlated with request mix' is exactly what missing admission control looks like; the hour of delay fits memory pressure building to the tipping point. Garbled output alongside memory errors widens the net: dtype or quantization mismatch on new weights, kernel/driver incompatibility, or hardware ECC errors - check dmesg and DCGM to rule the hardware in or out. Verify recovery with a canary replaying captured traffic plus golden-prompt output checks, not just error rates, since silent corruption is the scarier half of this incident. Postmortem: deploy gates get a memory-pressure load test and output-equivalence checks, and admission-control config becomes validated, versioned, and impossible to lose in a deploy.
rubric: Rolls back and recycles replicas, with the corrupted-process rationale
Connects intermittent OOM to lost admission control and the delayed onset to pressure buildup
Treats garbled output as its own signal: dtype/quantization mismatch or hardware, checked via dmesg/DCGM
Verifies with golden-output checks, not error rates alone, and hardens the deploy gate
followUps: What belongs in a pre-deploy load test to catch this class of regression?

questions.prompt: Given a large stream of events, return the k most frequent event types. Talk through your approach and its complexity - then how it changes when the counts no longer fit in memory.
questions.modelAnswer: In-memory: one pass building a hash map of counts, O(n) time, O(u) space for u unique types; then select the top k with a min-heap of size k - iterate the counts, push, and pop the minimum whenever the heap exceeds k - for O(u log k) selection and O(k) extra space, which beats a full O(u log u) sort when k is much smaller than u. A bucket-by-count array gives O(n + u) exact selection if you want to avoid the log factor. When counts exceed memory: partition by hash of the key across files or machines so every occurrence of a key lands in one shard, count exactly per shard, take each shard's top k, and merge - correct because a global top-k element must be a top-k element of its own shard. If it is a true unbounded stream, trade exactness for space: a Count-Min Sketch plus a k-sized heap gives bounded memory with one-sided overcount error, acceptable for trend detection but not for billing. I would also clarify requirements up front: tie handling, batch versus streaming, and whether approximate answers are acceptable - that last one halves the design space.
rubric: Correct O(n) counting plus O(u log k) heap selection with the k << u justification
Sharding argument is stated: hash partitioning makes per-shard top-k merge correct
Knows the exact/approximate boundary and what Count-Min error semantics allow
Surfaces clarifying assumptions: ties, streaming, exactness requirements
followUps: Why does taking each shard's top k stay correct, and when would it break?

questions.prompt: Design the public REST API for a model-inference platform: endpoints, versioning, sync versus async, and failure semantics.
questions.modelAnswer: Core resource: POST /v1/models/{model}/predictions. API version lives in the path and only breaking changes bump it; within a version, changes are additive. Model versions are a separate axis: callers may pin one explicitly, and every response echoes the resolved version so results are attributable and reproducible. Sync versus async by latency class: fast models answer synchronously under a hard timeout; long-running work returns 202 with a job resource - GET /v1/jobs/{id} for polling, webhooks for push - because holding connections for minutes fails at every proxy and mobile network between you and the caller. Failure semantics get designed, not inherited: idempotency keys on POST so client retries cannot double-execute or double-bill; a correct 4xx/5xx split - 400 validation, 401/403 auth, 429 rate-limited with Retry-After, 503 overloaded - because clients build retry logic off these codes; structured error bodies with stable machine-readable codes and a request ID for support. Round it out with pagination on list endpoints, per-key quotas and rate limits, published SLOs, and contract tests in CI so a 'small' response change cannot break integrators silently.
rubric: Separates API versioning from model versioning, echoing the resolved model version
Async pattern is correct: 202 plus job resource, with the connection-holding rationale
Idempotency keys and a deliberate 4xx/5xx mapping with Retry-After on 429
Includes observability and compatibility: request IDs, contract tests, SLOs
followUps: How would you introduce streaming responses without breaking existing clients?

questions.prompt: From a client typing an API URL to receiving JSON - walk through what happens at the network level, and how the layers map to the failures you see in production.
questions.modelAnswer: DNS first: local and OS caches, then a recursive resolver walks to the authoritative server, returning an IP. TCP handshake next - SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK - establishing a reliable byte stream. For HTTPS, the TLS handshake follows: negotiate protocol version and cipher, the server presents a certificate the client validates against trusted CAs and the hostname, and the two derive session keys. Only then does the HTTP request travel over the encrypted stream, typically hitting a load balancer that forwards to an application server, which returns status, headers, and JSON body. Connection reuse via keep-alive, and multiplexing in HTTP/2, exist to amortize those handshakes - and the request usually rides an already-open connection. The production value of this model is that failures name their layer: NXDOMAIN or resolution timeouts are DNS; connection refused or timeout is TCP - a dead service, a closed port, a firewall, or a security-group rule; certificate errors are TLS - expiry, hostname mismatch, or a missing chain; 4xx/5xx means the network is fine and the application is not. Debugging an outage is walking that ladder in order.
rubric: Covers DNS, TCP, TLS, HTTP in order with the essential purpose of each
Includes cert validation and where keep-alive/multiplexing fit
Maps failure symptoms to layers as a debugging ladder
Stays concise and correctly ordered under time pressure
followUps: Where does a connection pool's exhaustion show up in this picture?

questions.prompt: How do you structure tests for a service with ML components - what is worth testing at each level, and what is genuinely different from ordinary software testing?
questions.modelAnswer: The pyramid still applies: many fast unit tests on feature transforms and business logic, integration tests on pipeline and API contracts, and a few end-to-end smoke tests. The ML-specific differences are three. First, model outputs are statistical, so you test properties rather than exact values: output schema and ranges, invariants like monotonicity where the domain demands them, and metric thresholds on a fixed golden set - 'AUC at least X on this fixture' - with float tolerances and pinned seeds instead of assertEqual. Second, data gets first-class tests: schema and distribution validation on inputs, in CI against fixtures and in production against live traffic, because most ML failures arrive through the data path rather than the code path. Third, the model artifact is a versioned dependency: a candidate model bump runs the eval suite in CI exactly as a library bump runs unit tests, with a pinned tiny model keeping the rest of the service's tests fast and deterministic. Add a seeded one-epoch training smoke test so the training loop itself is covered - the classic gap where everything unit-passes while training silently broke.
rubric: Keeps the pyramid but converts model assertions to properties, invariants, and thresholds
Elevates data validation to a first-class test target in CI and production
Treats model updates as dependency bumps gated by evals in CI
Covers the training loop with a seeded smoke test, with determinism handled via pins
followUps: What flakiness sources appear in ML test suites, and how do you quarantine them?

questions.prompt: A feature branch is 30 commits behind main with conflicts. Talk through rebase versus merge for catching it up - and how you recover when a rebase goes wrong.
questions.modelAnswer: Merging main into the branch creates one merge commit, preserves history exactly as it happened, and resolves all conflicts in a single sitting - safe, if noisy. Rebasing replays the branch's commits on top of main for a linear history, but conflicts arrive commit by commit (resolve, git rebase --continue, or --abort to bail out cleanly), and it rewrites commit SHAs - which is why the iron rule is never rebase a branch others are building on, and why pushing afterwards requires force. Use --force-with-lease rather than --force: it refuses to overwrite remote work you have not seen, protecting a teammate who pushed in the meantime. Recovery is where git rewards understanding: the reflog records every previous HEAD position, so git reflog, find the pre-rebase entry, and git reset --hard to it restores the branch exactly - committed work is effectively never lost while the reflog lives. Also worth saying: if the team squash-merges PRs anyway, main's history is linear regardless, and the rebase-versus-merge debate on the feature branch is mostly aesthetics - team convention should win over personal taste.
rubric: Accurate mechanics of both paths, including per-commit conflict resolution and --abort
States the shared-branch rule and prefers --force-with-lease with its rationale
Recovery via reflog and reset is concrete and correct
Frames the choice as team convention, noting squash-merge makes it moot
followUps: When is git rerere worth enabling for repeated conflict resolution?

questions.prompt: Explain image versus container, and why containers displaced VMs for service deployment - including one thing VMs still do better.
questions.modelAnswer: An image is the immutable artifact: a layered filesystem plus metadata - entrypoint, env, exposed ports - built once and shipped everywhere. A container is a running instance of that image: a process (or process tree) on the host, isolated through kernel namespaces (pid, network, mount) and constrained by cgroups, with a thin writable layer on top; one image, many containers. Containers won deployment because they share the host kernel: no guest OS per instance means millisecond starts and dense packing, and the image pins the entire userspace dependency stack, giving dev-prod parity - the durable fix for 'works on my machine' - plus artifact-based rollbacks by redeploying the previous image. What VMs still do better is isolation: a hypervisor boundary with a separate kernel per guest is a far stronger security wall than a shared kernel, where a kernel exploit is a container escape; that is why untrusted multi-tenant code runs in microVMs like Firecracker, and why VMs remain the answer when you need a different OS or kernel than the host. The practical default: containers for your own services, VM-grade isolation where tenants are untrusted.
rubric: Image as immutable layered artifact versus container as namespaced process is precise
Names the shared-kernel mechanism behind speed and density, plus dev-prod parity
Correctly credits VMs with the stronger isolation boundary and the microVM middle ground
Gives the trust-based decision rule at the end
followUps: What actually happens at docker run - which namespaces and cgroups get created?

questions.prompt: A few heavy customers are hammering your inference API. Design rate limiting and caching for it: algorithms, where they live, and the failure modes of each.
questions.modelAnswer: Rate limiting: token bucket per API key - a capacity for bursts, a refill rate for sustained throughput - which serves real traffic better than fixed windows (burst-at-boundary artifacts) while staying simple to reason about. Enforce at the gateway with counters in a shared store like Redis using atomic operations, and decide the Redis-down behavior deliberately: fail open with conservative local limits for availability, or fail closed where overload is the greater risk. Return 429 with Retry-After and rate-limit headers so well-behaved clients back off on their own. Crucially for LLM APIs, requests are long-lived and wildly variable in cost, so per-second request rate is a weak control: cap concurrent in-flight requests per key, and meter token-denominated quotas separately from request rate - the monthly budget and the burst control are different mechanisms. Caching: an exact-match response cache keyed on a canonical hash of model, parameters, and input - but only for deterministic (temperature-zero) requests, because caching sampled outputs silently changes product semantics; below that, engine-level prefix caching accelerates shared system prompts for everyone. Failure modes to design against: unnormalized keys collapsing distinct requests (or missing identical ones), hot-key stampedes on popular prompts - request coalescing so one miss populates for all waiters - and per-tenant fairness inside shared cache capacity so one heavy customer cannot evict everyone else.
rubric: Chooses token bucket with burst/sustain reasoning and distributed atomic enforcement
Makes the fail-open/fail-closed call explicitly and returns actionable 429s
Recognizes long-lived variable-cost requests: concurrency caps and token quotas beside rate
Caches only deterministic outputs with canonical keys, and handles stampedes via coalescing
followUps: How do you communicate limits so heavy customers upgrade instead of churning?

questions.prompt: Ten minutes after your service deploy, the 5xx rate jumps from 0.1 percent to 8 percent and pages fire. What do you do, in order?
questions.modelAnswer: Roll back first, diagnose second: an error spike ten minutes post-deploy is the deploy until proven otherwise, rollback costs minutes while root-causing costs hours, and users are eating errors the entire time you investigate - if the change rode a feature flag, flipping it off is even faster. Verify recovery on the dashboards, post status so nobody duplicates the response, and preserve evidence: keep the bad build and capture logs and traces from the window. Then investigate at leisure: which endpoints and error codes, what the traces say, and the full diff of the deploy - code, config, dependency bumps, and migrations. Migrations are the trapdoor case, because rolling back code does not roll back a schema; that risk is designed away ahead of time with expand-migrate-contract so old and new code both run against the current schema, and it is why 'roll back' must be a rehearsed, known-safe operation rather than a hope. Afterwards, a blameless postmortem with a timeline, and the question that actually improves things: why did no gate catch it - and the fix is usually canary deploys with automatic rollback on error-rate breach, plus the missing test or alert, plus smaller deploys, since rollback-first only works when each deploy is small enough to be safely reversible.
rubric: Rolls back before diagnosing, with the time-asymmetry argument made explicit
Handles the migration trapdoor via expand-migrate-contract compatibility
Preserves evidence and communicates status during mitigation
Postmortem targets the missing gate: canary with auto-rollback, smaller deploys
followUps: What makes a rollback unsafe, and how do you audit for those conditions ahead of time?

questions.prompt: The service passes all tests locally and in CI, but returns 502s through the load balancer in production. How do you debug it?
questions.modelAnswer: A 502 is the load balancer telling you it could not get a valid response from upstream, so first split the problem at the LB: check target health status, and hit the app directly from inside the environment - exec into the pod or port-forward and curl localhost. If direct requests succeed while LB requests fail, it is wiring; if both fail, it is the app in this environment. The classic wiring causes: the app bound to 127.0.0.1 instead of 0.0.0.0 inside the container, so nothing outside the netns can reach it; a port mismatch between containerPort, service, and target group; or a health-check path returning non-200 so every instance gets marked unhealthy and pulled. App-in-this-environment causes: missing env vars or secrets in prod config, OOM crash-looping under a prod-sized memory limit it never sees locally, or an LB idle timeout shorter than a slow endpoint's response time. Read the LB's own logs - they distinguish connection refused from timeout from bad response, which cuts the hypothesis space in half immediately - and walk the request path hop by hop comparing config against what CI exercised, since CI almost never tests the LB-to-container wiring. Fix the class, not the instance: a post-deploy smoke test that hits the service through the load balancer.
rubric: Bisects at the LB with a direct-to-app request before guessing
Names the classic wiring causes: bind address, port mismatch, failing health checks
Uses LB logs' refused/timeout/bad-response distinction as evidence
Prevents recurrence with a through-the-LB smoke test in the pipeline
followUps: Which of these causes would a staging environment have caught, and which slip through to prod anyway?

questions.prompt: A teammate claims their training run is reproducible because they call torch.manual_seed(42) at startup. You need an independent team to reproduce the result next quarter. What would you actually record, and what level of reproducibility would you promise?
questions.modelAnswer: A seed is one small piece of a run's identity. To reproduce a run I record the full graph: the git commit plus a patch hash if the worktree was dirty, the fully resolved config, a data manifest with content checksums and the tokenizer version, the environment as a lockfile plus container image digest, the hardware and driver runtime, every RNG seed and state including data order and worker count, and the evaluator version with decoding settings. A seed without the RNG implementation, data order, and nondeterministic-kernel settings is not a complete randomness record. I would also be explicit about the level we promise: repeatability means the same team and setup gets the result again; reproducibility means an independent setup follows the documented procedure to a materially equivalent result; replicability means an independent implementation supports the conclusion. Bitwise equality is achievable for a tiny CPU fixture but usually neither portable nor necessary for a distributed accelerator run, so I define a contract stating which outputs must be exact, which are tolerance-bounded, and which only replicate directionally. To validate, I run a clean-checkout repeat: fresh clone, install only from the lock, verify input checksums, and compare against the contract - passing inside my own stale environment does not count.
rubric: Names run identity beyond the seed: commit plus patch state, resolved config, data manifest, environment digest, hardware, RNG states, evaluator
Distinguishes repeatability, reproducibility, and replicability rather than treating them as one promise
Treats bitwise equality as a declared contract - exact vs tolerance-bounded vs directional - not a default goal
Validates with a clean-checkout repeat from the lockfile, rejecting a pass in the developer's existing environment
followUps: Which sources of nondeterminism remain after every seed is fixed?
Why is recording dirty=true without a patch or content hash insufficient?

questions.prompt: Your experiment tracker stores metrics and hyperparameters, yet nobody can answer which data snapshot and evaluator version produced last month's best number. What does a complete experiment record contain, and why is a metric without that lineage weak evidence?
questions.modelAnswer: An experiment is more than a run, and a tracker that only stores metrics and hyperparameters captures the least durable layers. A complete record covers: the question - hypothesis, motivation, expected mechanism; code - commit, patch or dirty state, dependency and container digests; data - an immutable snapshot with filters, mixture, tokenizer, and order seed; model - architecture, initialization, parameter count, precision; training - optimizer, schedule, batch and token accounting, parallelism, hardware; evaluation - evaluator version, prompts, decoding, aggregation, and slices; outputs - checkpoints, logs, and sample predictions; and analysis - confidence, caveats, anomalies, and the decision taken. Lineage matters because a metric is a claim about a measurement procedure, not an intrinsic property of the model. If I cannot relate a number to its code, data, and evaluator, I cannot tell whether an improvement came from the intervention, a data change, or an evaluator change, so the number is weak evidence even when it looks good. Evaluator drift is especially sneaky: two scorer revisions can rank identical predictions differently. In practice I validate the system by picking a random reported number and proving I can reconstruct it end to end; if that audit fails, the tracker is a dashboard, not a record.
rubric: Covers the record layers: hypothesis, code identity, data snapshot and mixture, model, training, evaluation protocol, outputs, analysis
Includes evaluator version, prompts, and decoding as part of lineage, not just training metadata
Explains why an untraceable metric is weak evidence: intervention vs data vs evaluator changes become indistinguishable
Proposes an audit: reconstruct a reported number end to end from the record
followUps: How would you detect that an evaluator revision, not the model, moved a metric?

questions.prompt: You shipped a change that bundled a new auxiliary loss, a learning-rate tweak, and a data-mixture adjustment; the bundle gained 3 points on your primary eval. Your lead asks what actually caused the gain and gives you a limited compute budget. Design the ablation study.
questions.modelAnswer: First I decompose the bundle into atomic interventions, because the scientific unit is one change against a matched control that differs only in that change. With three components I would run the matched control with none of them, each single change, and the full bundle - pairwise combinations only if the singles fail to add up, since interaction is the usual reason they do not. Every run holds budgets fixed: parameter count, token budget, optimizer budget, and the evaluation protocol, so I measure the intervention rather than extra compute. I add a negative control - a change that should not matter - to detect pipeline artifacts, and I treat the learning-rate tweak with suspicion, since tuning often masquerades as a modeling win. One seed is an observation, not a distribution, so remaining budget goes into seed replication on the decisive comparisons rather than more variants; ten near-identical hyperparameter runs are less informative than one diagnostic ablation plus a replication. Where the mechanism predicts it, a dose-response run - sweeping the auxiliary loss weight - tests whether behavior follows the proposed explanation. Critically, I preregister the primary endpoint, the minimum meaningful effect, and the analysis and stopping rule before reading results, so I cannot rationalize noise into a story afterward.
rubric: Decomposes the bundle into single-change runs against a matched control, with budgets held fixed
Includes a negative control for pipeline artifacts and flags the learning-rate tweak as a confounder
Spends budget on seed replication of decisive comparisons, treating one seed as one observation
Preregisters endpoint, minimum meaningful effect, and analysis before results are read
followUps: When are pairwise interaction runs worth their compute?
How do you report the result honestly if only the full combination wins?

questions.prompt: Before committing a large compute budget to one pretraining run, your team wants to fit scaling laws on smaller models to choose model size and token budget. Walk me through the workflow, and the pitfalls that make scaling-law extrapolations mislead.
questions.modelAnswer: The workflow: train a grid of smaller models across sizes and token budgets with a consistent recipe - same data mixture, tokenizer, optimizer family, and schedule philosophy - then fit held-out loss against scale as a power law, with uncertainty on the fit. From that I identify the compute-efficient allocation between parameters and tokens and the apparent irreducible floor in this regime. The step teams skip is validating the extrapolation at an intermediate scale before betting the full budget: train one model between the grid and the target and check it lands on the predicted curve. Pitfalls: extrapolating across architecture, data, or optimizer changes invalidates the fit; too few correlated points gives false confidence; fitting training loss instead of held-out loss rewards memorization; repeated or low-quality data bends the curve; and lower loss does not uniformly improve the capabilities you actually care about, so downstream evals belong in the decision. Compute-optimal is also not deployment-optimal - inference cost scales with model size for the model's whole life, which often justifies training a smaller model well past its compute-optimal token count. Finally I sanity-check against utilization and dollar and time limits, because a theoretically optimal allocation the cluster cannot achieve is not optimal.
rubric: Describes the grid-fit workflow with consistent recipes and held-out loss, including uncertainty on the fit
Validates extrapolation at an intermediate scale before committing the full budget
Names concrete pitfalls: cross-recipe extrapolation, few correlated points, training-loss fits, data repetition
Separates compute-optimal from deployment-optimal, bringing inference cost and downstream evals into the choice
followUps: Why does data quality change the fitted exponents?
How would you detect the production run drifting off the predicted curve early?

questions.prompt: Twelve hours into a 256-GPU BF16 pretraining run, the loss goes NaN. Restarting from the last checkpoint hits NaN again a few hundred steps later. Walk me through your debugging playbook, and tell me why skipping the bad step is not a fix.
questions.modelAnswer: The deterministic recurrence is a gift: checkpoint plus data cursor reproduces the failure, so I can debug on a small, cheap replay instead of the full job. My playbook: stop at the first non-finite tensor using anomaly hooks on the replayed run, recording batch IDs, rank, step, and RNG and data cursor state. Then verify the boring layers first - inputs, labels, masks, and the loss denominator are finite and nonempty, since an all-masked microbatch dividing by zero looks exactly like an optimization blowup. Next inspect logits and loss before backward, then per-layer activation and gradient norms plus optimizer state to localize the layer; the NaN observed in the loss often originated many operations earlier. To separate numerics from logic, I rerun the bad batch in FP32 and on one device, and disable suspect fused or compiled kernels as a diagnostic. BF16 has FP32's exponent range, so overflow is less likely than with FP16, but invalid math and oversized updates still produce NaNs. Once the mechanism is fixed, I re-enable performance features one at a time. Skipping bad steps is not a fix because repeated skipping silently biases the data the model trains on and hides the root cause - it converts a loud failure into a quiet one.
rubric: Recognizes the reproducible replay from checkpoint plus data cursor and debugs on a small rerun
Checks inputs, masks, and the loss denominator before blaming optimization; knows the NaN origin precedes the loss
Bisects with FP32, single device, and disabled fused or compiled kernels; explains why BF16 still NaNs
Rejects step-skipping because it biases training and hides the mechanism; re-enables features one at a time
followUps: What would per-layer update-to-weight ratios add to this diagnosis?

questions.prompt: A 1,000-accelerator training run slowed 18 percent after your team enabled longer sequences and FSDP prefetch, yet average GPU utilization still looks healthy. As the on-call research engineer, how do you diagnose it and decide what to roll back?
questions.modelAnswer: First I would check what the 18 percent actually measures. Longer sequences change the work per step, so I compare actual loss tokens per second, not step time - the run may be doing more useful work per step than before. If tokens per second genuinely fell, I decompose the step: input wait, host and launch work, device compute, exposed communication, and checkpoint or eval amortization, using per-rank timelines, because a synchronous step runs at the pace of the slowest rank and average utilization hides tails. Longer sequences skew per-rank token counts and activation memory; FSDP prefetch adds transient all-gather buffers, so I look for allocator pressure - rising reserved memory, fragmentation, synchronizing frees - and for gather overlap that quietly stopped overlapping compute. Then I correlate straggler ranks with physical causes: input bytes per rank, storage node, CPU throttling, GPU clocks and thermals, network path, and link retries; a single slow host or one hot storage shard routinely taxes the whole gang. For the decision, I toggle one change at a time on a small replica and measure tokens per second and memory peaks; whichever change fails in isolation gets rolled back or retuned. I validate the fix on the big run against cost per token, not utilization, which was misleading from the start.
rubric: Questions the metric first: compares loss tokens per second, since longer sequences change work per step
Decomposes step time with per-rank timelines and states that synchronous steps follow the slowest rank
Connects FSDP prefetch to allocator pressure and gather overlap, and stragglers to physical causes

questions.prompt: You are asked to design the data pipeline for a new pretraining corpus built from a web crawl plus licensed sources. What stages sit between acquisition and training, and which decisions are science-critical rather than plumbing?
questions.modelAnswer: The pipeline: source governance first - rights, consent, allowed purposes, and sensitivity per source, because technical accessibility is not permission. Then an immutable raw snapshot with manifests carrying URIs, checksums, byte counts, schema, and policy tags, so every later transformation is reproducible. From there: parse and normalize; quality, language, safety, and privacy filters; exact and near deduplication; decontamination against evaluation benchmarks; mixture and curriculum; then tokenize, pack, and shard. Every arrow needs versioning, metrics, rejection samples, and an owner. The science-critical decisions are the ones that change what the model learns. Filter thresholds top the list - I insist on logging rejection samples because a quality filter silently deleting a dialect or a domain is a capability decision made by accident. Deduplication strength cuts memorization and wasted compute but can erase minority content. Decontamination protects the validity of every future eval. The mixture is empirical and objective-dependent, not something to set by intuition. Tokenizer choice is scientific too - it changes the unit of loss. I would validate the pipeline by ablating filters and mixtures at small scale before committing, auditing rejection samples by hand, and running a memorization audit after training so the findings feed back into curation.
rubric: Orders the stages: governance, immutable raw snapshot with manifests, filters, dedup, decontamination, mixture, tokenize and shard
Separates science-critical choices - filter thresholds, dedup strength, mixture, tokenizer - from plumbing
Names dedup's trade-off: less memorization and wasted compute vs erasing minority content
Validates with small-scale ablations, rejection-sample audits, and a post-training memorization audit
followUps: How do you version a mixture so a later run can reproduce it exactly?

questions.prompt: Your model jumps eight points on a public benchmark right after a new pretraining data drop. Before anyone announces the gain, what contamination and benchmark-overfitting checks do you run, and what claim can you honestly make afterward?
questions.modelAnswer: The timing is the tell: a jump coinciding with a data drop is a contamination hypothesis until ruled out. Public benchmarks leak into pretraining through the test sets themselves, papers quoting them, model-generated datasets, and even evaluation code. My checks: exact and near-duplicate matching of benchmark questions and solutions against the new data, with time-aware decontamination since data acquired after a benchmark's release is higher risk; scoring on a private or freshly rotated set the data drop cannot contain; and canary transformations - paraphrased or perturbed variants - where a contaminated model degrades far more than a generalizing one. I would also audit for benchmark overfitting on our side: repeated prompt and method selection against a fixed test set is contamination by process, so the primary metric, prompting, decoding, and stopping rule should be preregistered and access to the final test restricted. On the claim: contamination detection is incomplete, so I never announce proof of absence. The honest statement is bounded - the gain holds on held-out and perturbed variants, with match rates against the corpus and our exposure uncertainty documented. If the gain exists only on the public set and dies on fresh variants, the eight points measured our data pipeline, not the model.
rubric: Treats the data-drop timing as a contamination hypothesis and names leak paths beyond raw test sets
Runs exact and near matching, time-aware decontamination, private or rotated sets, and canary variants
Recognizes process-level overfitting: preregistered metrics and restricted access to the final test
States a bounded claim with exposure uncertainty and refuses proof-of-absence language
followUps: Why does a large gap on paraphrase variants suggest memorization rather than capability?

questions.prompt: Take an elementwise add of two FP32 tensors on a GPU. Estimate its arithmetic intensity, tell me whether fusing it into the neighboring kernel helps and why, and then walk me through how you would profile before deciding any of this matters.
questions.modelAnswer: Per element, the add reads two 4-byte inputs and writes one 4-byte output - 12 bytes moved for roughly one floating-point operation, so arithmetic intensity is about 1/12 of an operation per byte before cache effects. Against the roofline - attainable throughput bounded by the smaller of peak compute and bandwidth times intensity - that sits deep in the bandwidth-bound region, so the kernel runs at memory speed no matter how many FLOPs the GPU advertises. Fusion helps for exactly that reason: fusing the add into its producer avoids writing the intermediate tensor to HBM and reading it back, and saves a kernel launch - a mathematically identical computation gets faster purely through less data movement. But before optimizing anything I climb the profiling ladder: end-to-end phase timing first, then an operator trace with shapes, then the device kernel timeline, and only then kernel counters on a proven hot kernel - starting at the kernel level wastes time when the real bottleneck is data loading, Python graph breaks, or checkpoint I/O. Measurement discipline matters: GPU launches are asynchronous, so host wall clock around a launch measures enqueue time; I use device events with proper synchronization, warm-up, and fixed shapes and clocks. After fusing, I revalidate correctness across shapes and dtypes with absolute plus relative tolerance and confirm step time actually moved.
rubric: Computes roughly 1/12 op per byte from 12 bytes per element and identifies bandwidth-bound via the roofline
Explains fusion as an avoided HBM round-trip for the intermediate plus fewer kernel launches
Follows the profiling ladder from end-to-end timing downward rather than starting at kernel counters
Handles async launches with device events and warm-up, and revalidates with absolute plus relative tolerance
followUps: Why can a fused kernel end up slower despite moving less data?

questions.prompt: Design checkpointing for a month-long run on several thousand accelerators: what goes into a checkpoint, how do you write one safely while training continues, and how do you guarantee restore works when the cluster comes back with a different world size?
questions.modelAnswer: A complete checkpoint is more than weights: parameters and buffers, optimizer moments, scheduler and step counters, precision and scaler metadata, per-rank RNG states, the dataloader cursor and mixture state, config and tokenizer versions, and parallel layout metadata - miss the data cursor and every restart silently repeats or skips data. Save protocol: coordinate a logical step, write shards to a new versioned temporary prefix with per-shard checksums, shapes, and dtypes, require every rank to succeed, then publish a small manifest atomically. The manifest, not the directory, defines existence, so a half-written save can never be mistaken for a checkpoint; old versions are cleaned only after restore validation. For world-size changes, rank-local pickles tied to launch topology are the classic trap - I use a distributed checkpoint format that describes global tensors and their placements so restore can reshard under a different data-parallel layout. Checkpoint frequency is an optimization: expected lost work is roughly half the interval plus save and restart time, balanced against I/O and synchronization overhead; asynchronous saves shift that trade. I would keep elasticity simple, since restarting the whole gang from a valid checkpoint usually beats elastic membership for sharded layouts. Validation is a drill, not a review: kill a save mid-write and prove restore rejects it, then restore at a different world size and compare the next training step against a reference contract.
rubric: Checkpoint contents include optimizer state, RNG, dataloader cursor, and layout metadata, not just weights
Save protocol uses a versioned temp prefix, per-shard checksums, all-rank success, and an atomic manifest publish
Uses a resharding-capable format describing global tensors and names the rank-local pickle trap
Sizes the interval from expected lost work vs I/O cost and validates with interrupted-save and resharded-restore drills
followUps: When is asynchronous checkpointing worth its memory and complexity cost?

questions.prompt: A conv layer has a 3x3 kernel, stride 2, padding 1, and 32 output channels on a 64x64 RGB input. Give me the output spatial size and parameter count, then explain why stacking two 3x3 convs is usually preferred over one 5x5.
questions.modelAnswer: Output size: floor((H + 2P - K) / S) + 1 = floor((64 + 2 - 3) / 2) + 1 = floor(31.5) + 1 = 32, so the output is 32x32 with 32 channels. Parameters: C_out x C_in x K_h x K_w + C_out biases = 32 x 3 x 3 x 3 + 32 = 896 - notably independent of image size, which is the point of weight sharing: the same kernels slide over every location, giving translation equivariance. On stacking: two 3x3 stride-1 convs see a 5x5 receptive field, because the second layer's 3x3 window covers outputs that each already summarize a 3x3 patch of the input. For C channels in and out, two 3x3 layers cost about 18C^2 weights versus 25C^2 for one 5x5, and the stack inserts an extra nonlinearity between them - more representational depth for fewer parameters and less compute. The general receptive-field bookkeeping is r_l = r_(l-1) + (K_eff - 1) x j_(l-1), where the jump j multiplies by each layer's stride. In practice I sanity-check shape arithmetic with the formula rather than trusting a 'same' padding label, since even kernels and strides above 1 have framework-specific asymmetric behavior.
rubric: Computes the 32x32 output using the shape formula, not guesswork
Gets 896 parameters and notes the count is independent of image size due to weight sharing
Explains the two-3x3 stack: 5x5 receptive field, fewer weights (18C^2 vs 25C^2), extra nonlinearity
Shows receptive-field and jump bookkeeping or flags framework-specific padding behavior
followUps: How does dilation change the effective kernel size, and what artifact can it introduce?

questions.prompt: Before ResNets, adding layers to a plain deep CNN eventually made even training error worse. What problem do skip connections solve, how does y = F(x) + x change what a block learns and how gradients flow, and when does the skip path need a projection?
questions.modelAnswer: The failure was the degradation problem: past some depth, plain networks got worse on training error, so this was an optimization failure, not overfitting - a deeper net could in principle copy the shallower one and do no worse, but plain stacks could not find that solution. The residual block reframes the task: y = F(x) + x means the layers learn a residual correction relative to identity rather than a full transformation. If the best thing a block can do is nothing, representing F(x) near zero is easy - just drive weights toward zero - whereas learning an exact identity through stacked nonlinear layers is hard. For gradients, the additive skip gives backpropagation a direct path: the derivative of y with respect to x includes an identity term, so signal reaches early layers without being multiplied through every transformation, which is what lets networks of hundreds of layers train. The skip needs a projection - typically a 1x1 convolution - whenever shapes disagree: a change in channel count or a stride that downsamples, since mismatched tensors cannot be added. Preactivation variants move normalization and activation before the convolutions to keep the identity path even cleaner. To validate the story, I would compare training curves of plain versus residual stacks at matched depth and watch where the plain network degrades.
rubric: Identifies degradation as a training-time optimization failure, explicitly not overfitting
Explains the residual reframing: learning F(x) near zero is easier than learning identity
Describes the identity gradient path that keeps early-layer signal from attenuating
Knows the projection cases - channel or stride mismatch - and ideally the preactivation refinement
followUps: Why does normalization placement matter in the preactivation variant?

questions.prompt: Explain how a ViT turns a 224x224 image into a token sequence for a transformer encoder, then compare its inductive biases with a CNN's. Given a small labeled dataset and a tight latency budget, which would you reach for, and why?
questions.modelAnswer: A ViT splits the image into non-overlapping PxP patches - at patch size 16, a 224x224 image gives (224/16)^2 = 196 tokens. Each patch is flattened to a P^2 x C vector and linearly projected to the model width, which is exactly a convolution with kernel and stride P; position embeddings are added because attention itself is permutation-invariant, and a class token or mean pooling provides the global representation. Cost scales as O(N^2 d) in tokens: doubling resolution quadruples the tokens and multiplies attention score work by roughly 16, which is why patch size is the key compute knob and hierarchical or windowed variants exist for dense tasks. On inductive bias: a CNN bakes in locality, translation equivariance, and weight sharing, so it extracts a lot from limited data; a ViT starts with global content interactions and a much weaker image-specific prior, so it typically needs more data, stronger augmentation, or pretraining - but it scales well and models long-range structure from the first layer. For a small labeled dataset under a latency budget, I would start with a pretrained CNN, or at minimum a pretrained ViT fine-tuned rather than trained from scratch. The honest comparison is end quality, data cost, robustness, latency, and transfer on my task - not the slogan that attention replaces convolution.
rubric: Gets the patch arithmetic (196 tokens at 16x16 on 224x224) and the conv-with-stride-P equivalence
Explains why position embeddings are needed and the quadratic cost of resolution
Contrasts CNN locality, equivariance, and weight-sharing priors with the ViT's weak-prior, data-hungry regime
Makes a defensible small-data, low-latency call framed as an empirical comparison
followUps: What breaks when you fine-tune a ViT at a different resolution than it was pretrained at?

questions.prompt: Your detector emits 300 scored boxes for an image containing a dozen objects. Explain how IoU is computed and how greedy NMS filters those boxes, then give me two concrete failure modes of greedy NMS and what you might do about them.
questions.modelAnswer: IoU is intersection over union: the overlap area between two boxes divided by the area of their union, a scale-invariant overlap measure between 0 and 1. Greedy NMS: sort boxes by confidence, take the highest-scoring box, remove every remaining box whose IoU with it exceeds a threshold, then repeat with the next survivor until none remain. The threshold trades duplicate suppression against recall on close neighbors. Failure mode one: crowded scenes - two genuinely distinct, heavily overlapping objects, like pedestrians in a crowd, get merged because the weaker detection is suppressed as if it were a duplicate; soft-NMS mitigates this by decaying overlapping scores instead of deleting boxes outright. Failure mode two: the class-wise versus class-agnostic choice - run per class, two boxes of different classes can survive stacked on one object when only one should win; run agnostically, legitimate cross-class overlaps get eaten. There is also a systems cost: NMS is sequential postprocessing that adds real latency at serving time. The same IoU machinery reappears at evaluation, where AP matches predictions to ground truth at an IoU threshold, so the reporting convention - AP50 versus averaging 0.5 to 0.95 - matters. I would tune the NMS threshold on validation data for my scene statistics rather than inheriting a default.
rubric: Defines IoU correctly and the greedy sort-suppress-repeat loop with its threshold trade-off
Names the crowded-scene suppression failure and soft-NMS as a mitigation

questions.prompt: Design a semantic segmentation model for factory surface defects where defect pixels are well under one percent of each image. Walk me through architecture, the losses you would use for that imbalance, and the metrics you would refuse to report alone.
questions.modelAnswer: Architecture: an encoder-decoder with skip connections, U-Net style, because classification backbones throw away the spatial resolution segmentation needs - the skips reinject high-resolution features so thin defect boundaries survive decoding. Dilated convolutions or a feature pyramid buy receptive field without destroying resolution, and defects at multiple scales need multi-scale features. For the imbalance, plain pixel cross-entropy fails: with under one percent positives, predicting no-defect everywhere is a 99 percent accurate disaster. I would combine cross-entropy with a Dice or Tversky term, which optimize region overlap directly and let me weight false negatives above false positives - the asymmetry a defect application actually wants - plus focal weighting if easy background gradients still swamp training. Two pipeline details silently break this task: masks must be resized with nearest interpolation, since bilinear invents fractional labels along boundaries, and unlabeled or void pixels need an ignore index excluded from both loss and metric. On metrics: I refuse pixel accuracy alone - background dominance makes it meaningless - and report per-class IoU with mean IoU across classes, plus recall at the operating threshold for the defect class, since a missed defect and a false alarm carry very different costs. Validation is per-line and per-defect-type slices with an augmentation ablation, because production-line lighting shortcuts are exactly what these models learn.
rubric: Chooses an encoder-decoder with skips plus dilated or pyramid features, justified by resolution recovery
Handles imbalance with Dice, Tversky, or focal combinations and asymmetric error weighting, not CE alone

questions.prompt: You fine-tune a pretrained ImageNet backbone on 2,000 medical images. Training accuracy reaches 99 percent, validation barely beats chance, and a colleague's frozen-backbone linear probe outperforms your full fine-tune. Diagnose the likely causes and fix the recipe.
questions.modelAnswer: The linear probe beating full fine-tuning is the diagnostic gem: the pretrained features are useful, and my training procedure is destroying them. With 2,000 images and every parameter free, the model memorizes the training set - 99 percent train against chance validation is textbook overfitting - and an aggressive uniform learning rate wrecks pretrained representations before the small dataset can teach anything better. Before recipe surgery, though, I would check the boring failure: preprocessing mismatch. If my pipeline's normalization statistics, channel order, or resize interpolation differ from what pretraining used, the backbone receives inputs off its expected distribution and the comparison is confounded. Recipe fixes: freeze the backbone and train the head first, then progressively unfreeze with discriminative learning rates - smallest for early layers - add stronger regularization and augmentation appropriate to the modality, and early-stop on validation. Medical data adds a sharper worry: split validation by patient and site, because a model this overfit may be learning scanner or hospital markers rather than pathology, and a random split hides exactly that. Negative transfer is real when the domain mismatch is large, so if progressive fine-tuning still loses to the probe, I accept the frozen backbone. I would validate the final recipe with a freeze/unfreeze ablation and per-site slices, not a single aggregate number.
rubric: Reads probe-beats-finetune as the procedure destroying good features, on top of textbook overfitting
Checks preprocessing parity - normalization stats, channel order, interpolation - before recipe changes
Fixes with freeze-then-unfreeze, discriminative learning rates, regularization, and early stopping
Splits validation by patient or site against shortcut learning and validates via ablation and slices

questions.prompt: Sketch greedy NMS in pseudocode: inputs are boxes, scores, and an IoU threshold. State its complexity, then tell me what changes for class-wise NMS and what soft-NMS does differently. What edge cases would your tests cover?
questions.modelAnswer: Pseudocode: sort indices by score descending; while candidates remain, pop the highest-scoring box, append it to the keep list, compute IoU between it and every remaining candidate, and drop those above the threshold; return keep. IoU itself: intersection width is max(0, min(x2a, x2b) - max(x1a, x1b)), height analogously; intersection area divided by area_a + area_b - intersection. Complexity: the sort is O(N log N) and suppression is O(N^2) worst case when few boxes suppress each other - fine for hundreds of boxes, a real serving cost for tens of thousands, which is why NMS is often the postprocessing bottleneck. Class-wise NMS runs the loop per class; a tidy implementation trick is offsetting each class's coordinates by a large class-dependent constant so boxes of different classes can never overlap, letting one class-agnostic pass do class-wise work. Soft-NMS changes the suppression rule: instead of deleting overlapping boxes it decays their scores - linearly or with a Gaussian in IoU - and re-thresholds afterward, preserving detections in crowded scenes. My tests: empty inputs, a single box, identical boxes, degenerate zero-area boxes, tied scores, thresholds at 0 and 1, and above all the coordinate convention - xyxy versus xywh, normalized versus absolute - validated against a reference implementation, since convention bugs pass any unit test built on the same wrong assumption.
rubric: Produces a correct sort-pop-suppress loop with a correctly clamped IoU computation
States O(N log N) sort plus O(N^2) worst-case suppression and its serving implication
Explains per-class looping or the coordinate-offset trick, and soft-NMS score decay

questions.prompt: Walk me through how a text-to-image latent diffusion model is trained and sampled: the forward noising process, what the network actually predicts, why the diffusion runs in a latent space, and how classifier-free guidance trades prompt adherence against diversity.
questions.modelAnswer: Training: the forward process gradually corrupts an image with Gaussian noise under a variance schedule beta_t; the closed form x_t = sqrt(alpha_bar_t) x_0 + sqrt(1 - alpha_bar_t) eps lets me jump straight to any timestep. The network eps_theta(x_t, t, c) - historically a U-Net with timestep embeddings, now often a diffusion transformer over latent patches - is trained with a simple MSE to predict the added noise given the noisy input, the timestep, and the text conditioning; predicting x_0 or velocity are variants. Sampling starts from pure noise and iteratively denoises; DDIM-like and higher-order solvers cut the step count, trading quality and diversity against latency, and distillation or consistency methods compress steps further. The latent part: an autoencoder maps images into a lower-dimensional latent space and diffusion runs there, which slashes compute and memory since cost scales with spatial size - the price is decoder artifacts and lost fine detail. Classifier-free guidance: during training the condition is randomly dropped, so one model learns conditional and unconditional predictions; at sampling I combine them as eps_uncond + s * (eps_cond - eps_uncond). Higher s sharpens prompt adherence but reduces diversity and eventually saturates and distorts. For validation I keep a fixed prompt suite with human review - FID and CLIP score are both gameable proxies - and log sampler, steps, guidance, and seed, since cross-hardware determinism is not guaranteed.
rubric: States the forward closed form with alpha_bar and the noise-prediction MSE objective
Explains latent diffusion's compute motivation and its decoder-artifact cost

questions.prompt: We want zero-shot product tagging without training a classifier per category. Design a CLIP-style system: the contrastive training objective, how zero-shot classification works at inference, and the failure modes you would warn the product team about before launch.
questions.modelAnswer: Training: dual encoders - one for images, one for text - each producing a normalized embedding. For a batch of matched pairs, compute all pairwise similarities s_ij = u_i dot v_j / tau and apply a symmetric cross-entropy so each image scores highest against its own caption and each caption against its own image; every other example in the batch serves as a negative, which is why batch scale and the learned temperature tau matter so much. Zero-shot inference: embed each candidate tag through prompt templates like 'a photo of a {label}', ensemble the templates, and classify by cosine similarity between the image embedding and each class embedding, softmaxed with a temperature. The prompts are part of the model - they get tuned on a development set, never the test set. Warnings for the product team: web-pair training bias means popular categories work far better than niche ones; false negatives during training - many valid captions per image - blur fine distinctions; performance is prompt-sensitive, so a rewording can shift accuracy; and compositional queries involving counting, spatial relations, or attribute binding are systematically weak. I would ship with calibration plus an open-set threshold so out-of-catalog items abstain rather than mislabel, and validate on retrieval metrics sliced by category frequency before trusting any aggregate accuracy number.
rubric: Describes dual encoders with normalized embeddings and symmetric cross-entropy over in-batch negatives

questions.prompt: Design a pedestrian detection system for an embedded camera that must run at 30 frames per second on-device. Take me from data collection through model choice to the launch decision, and be explicit about every accuracy-versus-latency trade you make.
questions.modelAnswer: I start from the error costs: a missed pedestrian is catastrophic, a false alarm is friction, so the whole system tilts toward recall at a managed false-positive rate. Data: collect across sites, cameras, lighting, weather, and seasons, and split by site and time - a random split leaks camera-specific cues and inflates every number that follows. Model: an efficient one-stage detector; the dominant latency knob is input resolution, which trades directly against small-object recall - distant pedestrians are exactly the small objects - so I pick the lowest resolution that meets recall on the small-size slice, then apply quantization and possibly distillation from a larger teacher. The 30 fps budget covers the pipeline, not just the model: capture, preprocessing, inference, and NMS - which adds real postprocessing latency - measured on the actual device at p99 under thermal throttling, not as an average on a devkit. Evaluation: AP with a stated convention for tracking progress, but the shipping metrics are recall on size, occlusion, and lighting slices at the chosen operating point, plus calibration for downstream alerting. Launch: shadow deployment against the incumbent, regression gates per slice rather than on the aggregate, a defined fallback when confidence collapses, and drift monitoring, because new sites will not match the training distribution. The decision rule is explicit: no slice regresses on recall, and p99 end-to-end latency holds the frame budget on-device.
rubric: Anchors the design in asymmetric error costs and site/time-grouped splits against leakage
Trades resolution against small-object recall deliberately and uses quantization or distillation for the budget
Budgets end-to-end p99 on-device including preprocessing and NMS under thermal throttling
Gates launch on sliced recall regressions, shadow deployment, fallback behavior, and drift monitoring
followUps: When would you add a lightweight tracker instead of raising detector resolution?
